entries.title: You Have Dining Questions. Tom Sietsema Has Answers.
entries.summary: In his NOTUS debut, our award-winning food correspondent fields questions on where to eat on the Mall, D.C.'s best sushi deal, and his go-to restaurants right now.
entries.content:
When NOTUS reached out recently to ask me what I’d like to do, the first idea that came to mind was to host a regular Q&A with readers. During my 25 years as the food critic for The Washington Post, from which I took a buyout last summer, the most important hour of my work week was 11 a.m. Wednesdays, when I’d answer reader rants, raves and everything in between.

Ask Tom was a place where I tried to help people find what they wanted, learn something new, solve a dining dilemma. The online exchange was so popular that it often trumped Trump news. The interactions also gave me an immediate sense of what readers were thinking about, which led to a number of my best-read critic’s notebooks.

Besides, even after I left The Post, readers followed me with their questions. Why not create a dedicated forum for responding to them?

Welcome, then, to my new advice column, Talk to Tom, where I’ll be addressing your dining questions — every Thursday.

Got a gripe or concern? Something you’re curious about? Send me an email at TalkToTom@notus.com. Questions and comments may be edited for length. 

Why do so many American restaurants force us to eat in the dark? We are frequent travelers to Europe, where you can actually read the menu and see your food without using a flashlight.

A dim interior accomplishes several things. For starters, it tends to relax people, which makes eating feel more pleasurable and may encourage lingering (say, to order more drinks, a win for the restaurant). Darkness also has a way of compressing even large rooms, creating cocoons of space, at least mentally. Dim lighting can hide flaws, too, in the decor as well as on diners. Don’t we all look better away from klieg lights?

That said, a thoughtful restaurant provides sufficient illumination — and a menu with easy-to-read print — for diners to see what’s in front of them. I've long said, restaurateurs need to audition everything diners will touch or see — utensils, chairs, lights — before buying them.

I’ve got family coming to D.C. Is there a restaurant on the Mall you prefer?

For proximity to the museums and value, I’m partial to America’s Table Cafe inside the lower level of the National Museum of American History, which fuels between 6,000 and 8,000 visitors a week around this time of year.

Leading the kitchen: executive chef Mollie Kaufmann, who previously served as the culinary operations manager for World Central Kitchen, and who offers food more personal than the crowd-size suggests. (Quick, what other local cafeteria offers shrimp and grits, flavored as if you were in the South?) A recent lunch also embraced a snappy bratwurst striped with brown mustard and topped with tangy sauerkraut; a salad bar that goes beyond the expected; and appealing side dishes to accompany the generous entrees. Fresh-tasting apple-fennel coleslaw, mustard-punched baked beans, and pickled okra outperformed a plate of slightly dry smoked chicken thighs. Nodding to the season was a fine trifle sweetened with blueberries and peaches. I get hungry just typing that.

Lines tend to move fast, by the way, thanks to friendly cashiers. “You’re going to fall asleep, eating all that!” one of them teased two of us as we paid. Snare the right table, and you
can enjoy your meal with the Washington Monument as a backdrop — a twofer attraction.

Help settle a debate. I say it’s just as easy to open a $30 bottle of wine as a $300 bottle. An oenophile in my group thinks otherwise — and says the tip should be higher on the more expensive wine.

Much as I enjoy wine, which I tip on like the food it is — 20%, the industry standard — I seldom splurge on anything priced in the triple digits.

Regarding dearer bottles, I turned to ace wine consultant and former restaurateur Janet Cam, who thinks an extra 10% or so gratuity should be applied to wines in the $350 and up range. In those situations, she says, “expertise [is] expected.” Customers should receive proper stemware, “ideally finely made Riedel, Schott Zwiesel and Glassine,” she gives by way of example. “The thin lip of the glass affects the taste and perception of wine.”

Cam says the wine should be presented and tasted before the food arrives, as “food aromas enter the glass, distorting the perception of wine.” Higher-priced wine typically involves the sommelier’s “attention, knowledge, time in sourcing the wine” and storing it properly — conditions the wine authority says “should be considered and compensated” with “cash in the hand of the sommelier.”

In short, sourcing, storing and serving minor versus major wines requires different effort.

Sushi seems to be on everyone’s mind in the District these days. Unfortunately, I find many non-omakase meals to be exceedingly “spendy,” as you say in Minnesota. Can you recommend a spot that doesn’t cost the fish’s weight in gold? 

Let me introduce you to the youthful Kiyomi from Masaaki “Uchi” Uchino, who made a splash in Washington when he helmed the top-notch Sushi Nakazawa at the back of the late Trump hotel (now the Waldorf Astoria). Since April, the chef can be found behind a handsome wooden door at 1895 L St. NW, in a small dining room set off with woven balloon lights overhead and a counter ringed with 16 seats. “Japanese style,” says Uchino, “with American feel.” Friendly, in other words.

The lure: a parade of (seven) nigiri or hand rolls plus miso soup for a bargain $40. The pleasure might begin with pale pink tile fish, garnished with lime zest, on a pillow of warm rice, and continue with raw yellowtail, Spanish mackerel, beef-colored tuna streaked with veins of fat, and porgy splashed with lemon juice and a touch of sea salt. The last gets hit with a blow torch before Uchino places the morsel on a small slate plate in front of you.
IMG_0572.jpg (480x640, AR: 0.75)My neighbors on a recent weekday murmured in unison as they bit into salmon smoked in hay, a technique that elevates the flavor of the fish without masking it. Even if you go the sushi route, the drill includes a hand roll. (Make mine yellowtail ignited with citrusy yuzu, please.)

At present, the venue is walk-in only for lunch. Omakase, served on Friday night for $135 a person, is by reservation for two seatings and includes grilled and fried dishes while featuring mostly fish from Japan, says Uchino. Kiyomi, the chef’s sister’s name, translates to “pure beauty” — an apt way to describe a deal of a meal in the city.

Now that you no longer have an expense account, have your restaurant habits changed? 

For sure — but not necessarily for budgetary reasons. After decades of eating out, sometimes as many as 10 meals a week for work, I’m rekindling my love for cooking at home. (Meatloaf, roast chicken, composed salads, BLTs and eggs for dinner are my current jam.) While I remain curious about the restaurant scene, locally and beyond, I’m also free to eat wherever I want, not where I feel obliged to visit.

There are a handful of places I return to frequently, both because they’re easy to get to (close to home) and their menus are to my taste: Bombay Club and Casa Teresa downtown, Perry’s, Reveler’s Hour and Rye Bunny in Adams Morgan, Donsak Thai Restaurant in Woodley Park, and Buck’s Fishing & Camping near the senior Politics and Prose are where you might find me most often.

Finally, I’m probably drinking less than when I was out every night, too; a cocktail followed by a glass of wine. No more bottles of grape juice unless I’m with a group. My liver thanks me.

Two food lovers are heading to Iceland for several days. What shouldn’t we miss?

You’ll want to book in advance for the top draws, which include Dill, the first Icelandic restaurant to get a nod from Michelin; Ox, which offers the feel of a speakeasy; Moss at the Blue Lagoon, whose seasonal tasting menu focuses on New Nordic flavors and whose view embraces lava fields; and, for something different and more relaxed, Sumac Grill + Drinks. The last is a lively brasserie with a charcoal grill and twists on Middle Eastern accents. Suddenly, I’m hungry for Reykjavik again.

I have a hankering for Burmese food. Point me in the right direction.

Arlington — specifically Padaek, the largest of the area Thai and Laotian restaurants owned by chef Seng Luangrath. Her partner in the kitchen is Nyi Nyi Myint, a native of Yangon (formerly Rangoon) who recently added several flavors from his homeland to the menu. “There aren’t a lot of Burmese restaurants” in the area, Myint says of the decision to broaden the script.

Spring for the fermented tea leaf salad — a crunchy-tangy toss that includes shredded cabbage, tomatoes, nuts, lime juice and chiles — and the fish soup mohinga that’s considered Burma’s national dish. Once you start spooning into the steaming, turmeric-tinted mohinga — thick with thin rice noodles, a whole egg, shredded blue catfish, and crisp Lao squash fritters — it’s hard to stop. Fresh ginger, garlic and fish sauce weigh in with their charms, too.

Myint says he has more Burmese dishes to add after vacation. September can’t come fast enough for some of his fans.

entries.title: States Are in a ‘Fight to the Death’ for the Democratic Primary Calendar’s Top Spot
entries.summary: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan are expected to be early states, according to interviews with DNC members.
entries.content:
A last-minute, aggressive lobbying campaign is underway over the phone and through the media, as Democrats from a handful of states jockey to lead off the presidential nominating calendar.

South Carolina Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain appeared on Roland Martin’s YouTube show Monday to declare, “we’re first, and we maintain that.” At a private reception Wednesday night, Democratic National Committee members mingled with Nevada Sens. Jacky Rosen and Catherine Cortez Masto, while New Hampshire boosters reached DNC members with one-on-one phone calls.

The all-out push will culminate at the DNC’s Rules and Bylaws Committee meeting later this week. The 49-person panel is charged with setting the early-state window, ahead of what’s expected to be a wide-open and unwieldy Democratic presidential primary. Ahead of Friday’s meeting, tensions are already running high.

“It’s going to be a bloodbath,” said one of the members, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Most states represented have at least one or two members on the committee, and I think they’re all going to fight to the death for this.”

Interviews with nearly a dozen DNC Rules and Bylaws Committee members revealed some certainty about which states will likely be inside the early window — South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan — but not necessarily the order. South Carolina and Nevada appear to be front-runners for the first spot over New Hampshire, according to these interviews. Members aren’t sure if they’ll add a fifth state to the slate, though if they do, New Mexico and Virginia lead that discussion.

“I believe South Carolina is in a good position, and our vote count is good. We made the case in May to be first, and we’ve been talking to members ever since then,” said Spain, the South Carolina party chair. “I believe we have the votes, but I think Nevada is the next-highest vote-getter.”

Setting the presidential primary calendar is one of the DNC’s most consequential tasks ahead of the 2028 presidential primary, and the Rules and Bylaws Committee must contend with its own internal politics over which states to elevate or demote — triggering debates over racial diversity and representation.

Members said they hoped to recommend a slate by Friday and send it to a full vote of the DNC at their meeting in Austin, Texas, next month. At least a few members are pushing to delay the decision until after the upcoming midterms, though others insist they must wrap it up as soon as possible.

“We need to rip the Band-aid off,” said a second rules committee member. “We’re going to make people mad no matter what, and it’s not going to get any easier after the midterms.”

Reordering the slate also made people mad in 2022, when then-President Joe Biden eliminated Iowa as an early state, elevated South Carolina to first and added Michigan. The party came under pressure to shake up its calendar after the 2020 presidential primaries, when technical difficulties upended the Iowa caucuses and candidates criticized Iowa and New Hampshire for their lack of racial diversity.

“There’s real ramifications, long-term ramifications, if we don’t make the right decision on the calendar,” said Jaime Harrison, the former DNC chairman who also served as the South Carolina Democratic Party chair. “Black voters are paying very close attention to this.”
Jim Clyburn AP-26201819688914 (4320x2880, AR: 1.50)South Carolina’s boosters are making their pitch publicly and privately, sharpened by the Supreme Court’s decision to further gut the Voting Rights Act this spring. They also argue that South Carolina’s relatively cheap media market, compactness and majority-Black primary electorate will be the best proving ground for future presidential candidates.

In a letter to DNC members and obtained by NOTUS, Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina) warned in May that it would be a “profound mistake for our Party to retreat” from Black voters and Southern states in the nominating process, adding that South Carolina’s role in the nominating process “has been about ensuring that candidates engage deeply with the diverse coalition.”

Officials from Nevada are also campaigning aggressively to be first. They, too, leaned into their state’s racial diversity, particularly its Latino population. Over the last year, Nevada’s elected officials have made personal appeals to DNC members and frequently hosted events to promote the state. More than 20 Latino leaders and groups signed on to a letter Wednesday, urging members to elevate Nevada in order to “reverse” the trend of losing Latino voters to Republicans.

“Choosing Nevada to go first is a strategic decision, as we work to win back the coalition we need to win back the White House in ‘28,” said Daniele Monroe-Moreno, the Nevada Democratic Party chair. “That coalition of rebuilding has to be a broad coalition, which has to include Black voters, Asian voters.”

Some members have suggested that the battle for first may include horse-trading on a fifth addition to the line-up. If Nevada were selected to go first, then members may add Virginia, putting two Southern states in the early window. And if South Carolina were to go first, then they could add New Mexico, another western state with strong Latino representation.

But DNC members have raised concerns about Nevada’s mail-in balloting, which could delay the results of the primary. Monroe-Moreno said the Nevada secretary of state’s office is “implementing adjustments and improvements” to its mail-in ballot counting.

“It may take a little more counting than another state,” she said. “I want to make sure that everyone's votes are counted.”

Without a Democrat in the White House, the 49-person committee is charged with making its own decision on the calendar. DNC Chair Ken Martin has largely remained hands-off, but that could change over the next few days, the committee members said.

“I don’t think Ken needs any more headaches than he’s already got,” said one Democratic operative involved in the calendar process and granted anonymity to speak candidly.

The chaos of selecting a new calendar comes during a rocky year for the DNC. Martin has faced questions over his leadership after presiding over an incomplete autopsy of the 2024 election and staring down serious fundraising challenges. The Republican National Committee is sitting on $128 million in cash, while the DNC holds $16.3 million with $18.5 million in debts, according to the most recent Federal Elections Commission filings.

It’s not clear whether states or candidates will follow the DNC’s decision on the primary calendar, given the committee’s weakened position. At least three potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates told NOTUS last month they were considering skipping the DNC’s debate schedule, while Iowa’s backers have already said they are seriously considering hosting a rogue caucus. 

Last month, the DNC instituted stiffer penalties if a state jumps the line to head off these challenges. For example, if a candidate campaigns in a rogue contest, they’ll sacrifice debate stage access and the state will lose its delegates at the party’s 2028 convention.

New Hampshire already tested those boundaries in 2024, when it ran its own unsanctioned primary after Biden demoted the state from its first-in-the-nation status. The state is still expected to be in the early window, but several DNC members said “New Hampshire is a very distant third” behind Nevada and South Carolina for first. “They just don’t have the votes,” a third DNC member said.

New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Raymond Buckley defended the state’s position, arguing in a statement that “anyone who suggests New Hampshire isn’t in a strong position is mistaken.”

“We’ve been focused on having conversations one-on-one with committee members, and we’re encouraged by how those have been going,” Buckley continued. “New Hampshire serves as a critical testing ground for whether candidates can attract independent voters — an issue that couldn’t be more pressing for the Democratic Party nationally.”

entries.title: Five Players to Watch at Commanders Training Camp
entries.summary: Washington opens camp next week, and these players have plenty to prove ahead of a new season.
entries.content:
Let’s get this out of the way: You’re not here to read about Jayden Daniels or Terry McLaurin or Laremy Tunsil or Sonny Styles. We all know they’re vital to the Commanders’ success this season.

But there’s about 70 other guys reporting to Ashburn for training camp next week, and they could very well dictate whether Washington makes a deep playoff run like it did in 2024 or goes 5-12 like last season.

Before the pads come out next week, here are five (fine, technically six) key players to watch in the home stretch of the offseason.

Nick Allegretti, center

The Commanders are set to return 80% of the starters on their offensive line: tackles Tunsil and Josh Conerly and guards Chris Paul and Samuel Cosmi. The only change will be at center, where Allegretti is expected to replace Tyler Biadasz, who was released back in March.

Allegretti has spent most of his eight-year NFL career at guard, including five seasons with the Chiefs. But he’s played center since childhood and was a top center prospect coming out of high school, according to 247Sports. He spent time at both center and guard over four seasons at Illinois.

While the offensive line has continuity on its side, it wasn’t exactly the best unit in the NFL last season: ESPN placed the group in the bottom half of the league in its run- and pass-block rankings. Allegretti started last season at guard while Cosmi recovered from injury, but he was removed from the starting unit after just two games. Allegretti has said he’s sat in on center-quarterback meetings since signing in 2024, and he put that experience into practice by starting the last two games of the season at center.

There’s reason to believe the Commanders feel optimistic about Allegretti. They signed him to a multi-year contract extension in March after letting Biadasz go, waited until the sixth round of April’s draft to take a center (Michigan State’s Matt Gulbin) and didn’t add any veteran competition in free agency.

Trey Amos, defensive back

They say the best ability is availability. Another popular idiom: You have to see it to believe it.

Both of those apply to Amos. The second-year cornerback didn’t participate in organized team activities (OTAs) or minicamp in June after fracturing his fibula during a Week 10 loss to the Lions.

Amos proved last season he’s one of, if not the best one-on-one defender in Washington. He allowed just one touchdown in coverage last season, and his six pass deflections ranked third on the team despite the fact that he appeared in just nine and a half games. He played particularly well against the Packers in Week 2.

The Commanders need Amos’ speed and physicality. Last season’s pass defense was more accommodating than an AirBnB host, allowing the second-most pass plays of 40 yards or more.

It’s not clear how Washington feels about Amos’ recovery, but it’s apparent the team is focused on the secondary: Earlier this month, they signed veteran Rasul Douglas to a one-year contract. Douglas started 13 games for the Dolphins last season and was one of the better lockdown defenders in football last season with 13 pass deflections and a 54% completion percentage allowed in coverage.

For what it’s worth, Amos said on a Twitch stream last week that he’s healthy and ready for training camp, according to the Full Command Youtube channel.

Croskey-Merritt Commanders AP - 25359693243378 (8367x5578, AR: 1.50)
Bill Croskey-Merritt, running back

On paper, Croskey-Merritt had as good of a 2025 season as could be expected of a seventh-round draft pick who played one game in his final season of college ball. He finished with a team-high 805 rushing yards and eight touchdowns.

But look closer and you can see areas Croskey-Merritt will need to improve. He lacked the pass-catching skills and explosive runs that make an offense dangerous: Of players with 800 or more rushing yards last season, he ranked last in receptions (9) and receiving yards (68) and tied for last in rushes of 20 yards or more (3). Croskey-Merritt also tied for the third-most fumbles (3) by a running back.

If the second-year back, who has visibly bulked up this offseason, wants to be more of a bell cow than a member of a committee, he’ll have to prove it in these coming weeks. And that’s not me talking, that is his head coach: After minicamp, coach Dan Quinn said he wanted to see improvement from Croskey-Merritt in pass-catching and explosiveness, and foresees him splitting reps with the other backs, including free agent signee Rachaad White (205 receptions, 1,450 receiving yards and 11 receiving touchdowns in four seasons with Tampa Bay).

“I do like the competition in the group,” Quinn said. “I think we'll for sure be more than just one [running back].”

Leo Chenal, linebacker

Seeing as most Americans choose the Super Bowl as the one NFL game they watch each season, Chenal’s name should sound familiar. In the Chiefs’ championship wins in 2022 and 2023, he totaled 12 tackles, two tackles for loss, a forced fumble and one quarterback hit. The linebacker, who signed a three-year deal with the Commanders this offseason, stuffed All-Pro 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey at the line of scrimmage on a third-and-2 in the fourth quarter of Super Bowl LVIII.

That nose for the football is desperately needed in Washington. The Commanders missed the second-most tackles (131) in the NFL last season, according to Pro Football Reference. Chenal’s 5.2% missed-tackle rate is the lowest among linebackers since 2023, per Next Gen Stats.

Chenal will be battling for first-string camp reps with first-round draft pick Styles and returning starter Frankie Luvu, but his ability to pursue, cover tight ends in coverage and fight through offensive linemen should go a long way towards improving a defensive unit that has struggled the past three seasons.

Antonio Williams and Treylon Burks, wide receivers

To paraphrase the immortal words of Rick Pitino: “Brandon Aiyuk ain’t walking through that door.”

For all the chatter about the Commanders needing another receiver ahead of training camp, it seems pretty clear they’re rolling with what they currently have. Which means someone has to line up opposite McLaurin, and it would appear Williams, a 2026 third-round pick, and Burks, a 2022 first-rounder in Tennessee, have the upper hand.

During 7-on-7 and 11-on-11 drills at OTAs and minicamp, Williams and Burks got a lot of time working with quarterbacks Daniels and Marcus Mariota.

Williams was primarily used out of the slot at Clemson last season, and his production didn’t exactly scream modern NFL starter (55 receptions, 604 yards, 11.0 yards per reception). But he is versatile and slippery, often used in jet sweeps and screens that take advantage of his speed. Much like most of the rest of the receiving corps, Williams is not a deep threat, but he can feast on defenses in intermediate routes.

Injuries have derailed Burks’ career, limiting him to just 35 games played in the last four years. But he’s shown big-play ability, albeit in spurts.

If Williams can find gaps in coverage and Burks can stay healthy, there’s a good chance one of them will earn a starting spot by the end of camp.

entries.title: States Are Struggling to Replace the Election Cybersecurity Infrastructure Trump Dismantled
entries.summary: Election officials from across the country say the administration has pared back support.
entries.content:
Top state election officials are warning the federal government is not doing enough to help states prepare for the possibility of cyberattacks ahead of the midterm elections.

President Donald Trump has had an unflinching focus on election integrity issues, which he has pushed Congress to address through legislation that would tighten voter-identification requirements.

In the meantime, several state officials told NOTUS that the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which supports state and local election offices in their efforts to bolster security against hackers, has stopped providing regular intelligence briefings as well as cut technical assistance and financial support for election administration to their states.

“The federal government knows that there are nation-state actors desperately trying to come after us and cause chaos in our elections, yet, they are reducing resources,” Steve Hobbs, Washington’s Democratic secretary of state, told NOTUS. “We're doing everything we can to try to protect ourselves with far less resources than we did before.”

Republican state election officials confirmed that the cuts have also changed their states' cybersecurity operations.

“If you go back to 2020, we had 30 different federal threat briefings. This year we received none,” Brad Raffensperger, Georgia’s Republican secretary of state, told NOTUS. “We benefited from that regular coordination with CISA. It was just another set of eyes with extended reach over the horizon and that many times our state agencies just don't have that available to them.”

“We know that there's a lot of threats currently between the Ukraine war and Russia not being pleased with our response there,” Raffensperger said. “The ongoing situation with Iranians, and then obviously AI has opened the door to a host of bad actors.”

The administration has aggressively reduced election-security personnel within CISA since Trump returned to office. Earlier this year, Congress cut hundreds of millions of dollars from CISA’s budget. The White House has proposed even deeper cuts to the agency’s budget.

The results of that are playing out as states prepare for the midterms. Three state election officials told NOTUS that CISA has stopped providing election-focused cybersecurity support and does not have the same capacity to operate as a central hub for state officials to communicate with federal agencies and to other states during cyberattacks.

Attempted cybersecurity attacks happen frequently, including during the 2024 election.

“The federal government has abandoned a large share of its previous commitment to helping states administer secure elections,” Steve Simon, Minnesota’s secretary of state, said. “There are a host of services that they previously provided under multiple administrations — including the first Trump administration — that are no longer available to us.”

Abigail Jackson, a White House spokesperson, did not respond to questions about the decrease in federal cybersecurity support for elections. Instead, her statement focused on the Trump administration’s efforts to clamp down on noncitizen voting.

“President Trump is committed to ensuring that Americans have full confidence in the administration of elections, and that includes totally accurate and up-to-date voter rolls free of errors and unlawfully registered non-citizen voters,” she wrote.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told NOTUS in a statement that under President Joe Biden, CISA had a “ballooning budget” that concealed “censorship, branding, and electioneering.”

“Under Secretary Mullin, CISA is focused squarely on executing its statutory mission,” this spokesperson wrote. “We are committed to delivering timely, actionable cyber threat intelligence, supporting federal, state, and local partners, and defending against both nation-state and criminal cyber threats.”

Many states have been forced to create and fund their own resources to replace federal services. For example, Simon told NOTUS that Minnesota substituted cybersecurity testing and tabletop exercises provided by the federal government with ones provided by private sector partners.

Still, there are some functions the federal government provided that states can’t compensate for.

“States, including very much Minnesota, have found ways to backfill and replace almost all of those services,” Simon said. “One area that is very difficult to replace is intelligence briefings. That is not something that we can just go to a store and buy.”

Geoff Hale, a former CISA election security official who worked at the agency during the Trump and Biden administrations, said that CISA is retreating from election security at a time when elections are at greater risk of being targeted by foreign adversaries like Russia, China and Iran.

“Iran has been so aggressive towards elections and election infrastructure over several election cycles,” Hale, who was laid off from CISA last year and is now a visiting fellow at the Center for Democracy and Technology, told NOTUS. “If they were willing to take those actions during better times when the relationship was not an ongoing war, I'm very fearful of what they'd be willing to attempt amid ongoing conflict.”

States also now have to fund a service that shares cybersecurity information across state lines, something the federal government used to pay for. Last year, the Trump administration ended funding for the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center, which is part of a nonprofit that helps the federal government share cybersecurity information with local election officials. While the organization continues to operate, it has faced staffing cuts which have limited its capabilities.

Officials from Georgia, Minnesota, Washington and New Mexico told NOTUS they’ve had to pay MS-ISAC fees this year.

“If something occurs in New Jersey, can Virginia benefit from understanding and blocking those suspicious indicators? Can Colorado and Texas benefit from information that occurred on systems in Ohio?” Hale asked. “It may not stop everything, but it stops an attack from getting much bigger.”

Several secretaries of state made a point of emphasizing to NOTUS they’re confident that their states have built up their own cybersecurity operations sufficiently to protect against cyberattacks this election cycle.

“We feel like we've been working on our capabilities over many years, and our voters can remain confident that Georgia is prepared to conduct secure, accurate and reliable elections,” Raffensperger said.

One official from a Republican-led state told NOTUS he’s not concerned about the lack of federal support ahead of the midterms.

“Our phone is always open to any calls from the Department of Homeland Security,” Denny Hoskins, Missouri’s secretary of state, told NOTUS. “I have the utmost confidence in President Trump and his administration that they can help sniff out these bad actors and handle any malicious attacks that occur across the U.S.”

Still, he acknowledged this is a high-threat environment for election infrastructure.

“We have cyberattacks on our election files as well as our business services files every day. I mean, every day we have bad actors that are trying to hack into those files,” Hoskins said.

CISA funding has been a point of contention in Congress for years. Trump and many congressional Republicans have argued that CISA’s efforts to track election misinformation amounted to federal overreach and a violation of the First Amendment. The Trump administration has framed cutting CISA funding as a way to focus on other areas of infrastructure cybersecurity.

“It is necessary to rescope the agency's election security activities to ensure CISA is focused exclusively on executing its cyber and physical security mission,” Bridget Bean, CISA’s acting director, told employees in a memo reported by Wired in February.

In May, Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia) wrote a letter to Kristi Noem, the DHS secretary at the time, to share his concerns about pulling back federal election support.

“I am gravely concerned about the lack of critical federal support to state and localities ahead of the 2026 midterms,” Warner wrote. “It is vital that CISA be permitted to respond to election threats, vulnerabilities, and foreign interference or influence.”

For some state election officials, however, the lack of federal support does not mean election security has reverted to where it was in 2016, when Russia was accused of interfering in the election to help Trump win the presidency.

“We're not back in 2016. We all learned the lesson of 2016, which is we have to double down and triple down on election security of all kinds. States have been doing that,” Simon said. “I would say that the federal government mindset has gone back in the time machine. But in terms of readiness, we are not in 2016. We are far more advanced than that.”

entries.title: Labor Pains
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Medicaid changes hit a D.C. hospital, the House advances a bill restricting home rule and Tom Sietsema answers your dining questions.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

THE LATEST

One of D.C.’s largest hospitals will shutter one of its two postpartum wards on Sunday. It’s the first health provider in the District to reduce service citing, at least in part, recent changes to Medicaid.

“Similar to hospitals nationwide, we are facing increasing financial pressures, including significant changes in Medicaid that affect all our services,” a spokesperson for MedStar Washington Hospital Center told NOTUS, adding that D.C.’s birth rate is also steadily declining.

President Donald Trump’s “one big beautiful bill,” passed last summer, cut more than $900 billion from Medicaid and changed its eligibility requirements. D.C. officials estimated 95,000 residents were at risk of losing coverage, and the District has seen a 9% reduction in enrollment in the past year.

“We do have a lot of patients on Medicaid,” one nurse in MedStar’s postpartum unit, Mel Rode, told NOTUS, adding: “We deliver 1 in 3 babies in the District and so, by closing a whole third of the postpartum beds, you are putting so many babies and so many delivering parents and mothers at risk.”

The hospital saw a 17% decline in newborn admissions this past year, but Rode said that both of its postpartum units have been over capacity multiple times this summer.

Council member Christina Henderson, who chairs the health committee, wasn't surprised to hear Medicaid could be a factor in the closing. But Janeese Lewis George, D.C.’s likely next mayor, cast doubt on how culpable it could be for the decision.

“Most Medicaid cuts have not yet gone into effect,” Lewis George told NOTUS in a statement. “MedStar's decision to close its postpartum delivery unit at Washington Hospital Center is a policy decision — one that must be reversed because of the critical role these units play in maternal health outcomes.”

Henderson said the hospital has no immediate plans to repurpose the unit and could reopen beds if patient numbers recuperate.





FROM THE DISTRICT

No new taxes, D.C. That’s the message a House committee sent Wednesday when it advanced a bill that would broadly restrict the city’s ability to increase taxes or fees. Martin writes that Republicans say the measure is intended to help the city become more economically competitive, while city officials counter that it would “straightjacket” them.

While D.C. officials loudly criticized Republican House members over the vote, another unexpected target emerged: DoorDash. The food-delivery platform supports the bill, largely over its opposition to a 20-cent delivery fee the D.C. Council recently approved. Some advocacy groups are calling on residents to boycott DoorDash, and social media has shown several people doing just that.

A high-profile lawsuit against D.C. over its ban on firearm magazines that can hold more than 10 bullets is on hold — for now. The plaintiff in the case and D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb have agreed to pause litigation pending a pair of cases the U.S. Supreme Court is expected to hear this year on the constitutionality of state laws banning AR-15 assault rifles, which D.C. similarly prohibits.

Agriculture Department workers say mandatory relocations from Washington to regional offices are mass layoffs in disguise, NOTUS’ Tyler Spence, Eric Katz and Natalie Alms report.

The Trump administration and D.C. Council finally have something they can agree on: razing the 11-acre Forrestal Building in Southwest D.C., City Cast DC reports.





TALK TO TOM

Tom Sietsema is here to answer your burning questions about the D.C. dining scene. 

Sietsema, a James Beard Award winner, is NOTUS’ food correspondent. Previously, he was The Washington Post’s food critic for 25 years.

Got a question for Tom? Submit them here. Each Thursday, we’ll turn this section over to him to give you some answers.

Question: I’ve got family coming to D.C. Is there a restaurant on the Mall you prefer?

For proximity to the museums and value, I’m partial to America’s Table Cafe inside the lower level of the National Museum of American History, which fuels between 6,000 and 8,000 visitors a week around this time of year.

Leading the kitchen: executive chef Mollie Kaufmann, who previously served as the culinary operations manager for World Central Kitchen, and who offers food more personal than the crowd size suggests. (Quick, what other local cafeteria offers shrimp and grits, flavored as if you were in the South?) A recent lunch also featured a snappy bratwurst striped with brown mustard and topped with tangy sauerkraut; a salad bar that goes beyond the expected; and appealing side dishes to accompany the generous entrees. Fresh-tasting apple-fennel coleslaw, mustard-punched baked beans and pickled okra outperformed a plate of slightly dry smoked chicken thighs. Nodding to the season was a fine trifle sweetened with blueberries and peaches. I get hungry just typing that.

In the full Q&A: Where to find the best sushi in D.C., why American restaurants are always so dark, how to tip on expensive wine, and more.





SPORTS

The Commanders open training camp next week, meaning football season is suddenly around the corner. NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson takes a look at five players with a lot on the line in Ashburn, including a young pass-catcher and a newly arrived Super Bowl champ.

The Nationals have started calling some pitches from the dugout, The Athletic reports, with Washington becoming the latest team to break a baseball norm in search of an analytical advantage.

entries.title: The Unknowns
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Trump threatens Iran’s civil infrastructure — again. The House and Senate prepare for war powers votes. A fight brews at the DNC over which state goes first. Congress earns its paycheck. Darline Graham faces an “unknown” problem. And: state election officials sound the alarm.





THE LATEST

The next stage: “I don’t know what the objectives are, so it’s kind of hard to measure what success is,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic yesterday after attending the return of four fallen U.S. service members at Dover Air Force Base. “I know what success isn’t — going to Dover like I did today and seeing the service members coming back.”

The term “forever war” has been thrust back into the zeitgeist, punctuated on Wednesday when U.S. Central Command launched the 12th consecutive day of airstrikes hours after Donald Trump attended his third dignified transfer since the Iran war began. He later called it the “toughest thing” he has to do as president.

Bridges and power plants. Those are the next targets near Tehran, according to Trump, who threatened to train the U.S.’s military might on a new civilian infrastructure target in retaliation for every boat Iran strikes in the Strait of Hormuz. While the president has made similar claims before (and then backed down), these new claims carry more heft as the war escalates.

The rhetoric is also escalating. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament, wrote on X, “In a region where we do not sell oil, no one will sell oil. If our security is not ensured, no infrastructure will be safe, and the security of the strait is in the absence of American forces.”

Another front: Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility for missile and drone attacks against two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, just days after announcing a blockade against Saudi Arabia, The Guardian reports.

The House and Senate are expected to vote — yet again — this morning on a war powers measure to curtail the president’s war as his language ratchets up.

Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia), who has opposed previous resolutions restricting war powers, told NOTUS’ Manuela Silva that civilian targets should be off the table: “I don’t want anything to do with blowing up the bridge. And when you blow up the bridge, you’re going to have civilian casualties for sure. Nobody wants that. Nobody in the world wants that, but what are you going to do?”

Open tabs: The Next Big Tests for the Left: Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota (NYT); OpenAI blamed a hacking event on its AI models going rogue (AP); U.S signs nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia that gives it path to enriching fuel (WaPo); Maine Democrat Troy Jackson has raised $1M for his Senate bid so far. (Politico)





From the campaign trail 


Fight Club, DNC edition: Democrats are preparing for battle as a handful of states jockey to lead off the presidential nominating calendar for 2028. That lobbying campaign is being waged through phone calls and media attention, NOTUS’ Elena Schneider reports.

“We’re first, and we maintain that,” Christale Spain, the chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party, said on journalist Roland Martin’s YouTube show Monday. South Carolina, where voting Democrats are majority Black, is locked in a tense fight to go first with Nevada, with its strong Latino constituency. The Rules and Bylaws Committee meets Friday to make its recommendation.

“It’s going to be a bloodbath,” said one of the members, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Most states represented have at least one or two members on the committee, and I think they’re all going to fight to the death for this.”

First on NOTUS: NRDC’s midterm play. The political spending arm of the Natural Resources Defense Council plans to spend more than $6 million this cycle on ads aimed at flexing environmental voter muscle. While the topic has been ignored of late in favor of fights over who can lower energy prices the fastest by any means necessary, the NRDC’s new ads try to connect those dots with data-center politics.

The first spots are going up in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District against Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan, a top target for Democrats. The ads have a podcast bro-y energy — pretty different from the earnest “In the Arms of an Angel”-style environmental appeals of old. One spot focuses on stock trading, specifically on Bresnahan’s purchase of stock in a data-center supplier.

From the Hill


A day in the life: The House finally did what few believed possible just a few weeks ago: pass some big-ticket legislation. House Republicans banded together with a 216-214 vote to ram through the third reconciliation package this term, this one coming in at $95 billion, NOTUS’ Stephen Neukam reports. Democrats banded together to oppose the funding for the war in Iran, farm aid and grants incentivizing states to adopt restrictive voter-ID laws on their own.

The House also passed (with some Democratic support) the $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act to muscle through Trump’s plans for the Pentagon and the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would curb members of Congress and their families from purchasing individually traded stocks.

Now, it’s the Senate’s turn, but don’t hold your breath for all of it: the chamber is historically not in a rush.

Speaking of that side of the Capitol, Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) is officially in the race to succeed her late brother, Lindsey Graham, but the question still remains: what does she believe? NOTUS’ Igor Bobic, Al Weaver and Oriana González report on the quandary facing Republicans who don’t personally know Graham or where she stands, despite wholeheartedly endorsing her.

“These are people with legislative records that they can point to, that are proven to say, ‘Hey, prices are up, we can bring prices down if we do X, Y and Z. Here’s what I’ve done in the past,’” CJ Westfall, chair of the Dorchester County Republican Party, told NOTUS. Darline Graham is “somebody that’s unproven and just has the stamp of approval by the president. I don’t think that’s the end-all, be-all for South Carolina.”





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

A savvy social-media campaign — dubbed Nixonmaxxing — has made Richard Nixon cool again. Today at NOTUS Perspectives, Matt K. Lewis writes about why this is happening now and why it’s a good thing.





NOTUS METRO

NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter!

In his NOTUS debut: You Have Dining Questions. Tom Sietsema Has Answers.

Sports desk: Five Players to Watch at Commanders Training Camp, by Martenzie Johnson





NEW ON NOTUS

Trump says he wants election security beefed up, but some election officials are questioning why the federal government is failing to help protect states from possible cyberattacks ahead of the midterms, NOTUS’ Samuel Larreal reports.

“The federal government knows that there are nation-state actors desperately trying to come after us and cause chaos in our elections, yet, they are reducing resources,” Steve Hobbs, Washington state’s Democratic secretary of state, told Sam. “We’re doing everything we can to try to protect ourselves with far less resources than we did before.”

entries.title: A Decades-Old Terrorist Deportation Court Is Being Used for the First Time
entries.summary: Judges on the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, created in 1996, have never heard a case — until now.
entries.content:
The Justice Department’s decision last week to activate a terrorist deportation court for the first time in its 30-year existence has surprised the judges who once sat on this dormant tribunal — and long wondered what hearings would even look like.

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court is a little-known and untested venue for the government to deal with terrorism suspects in the U.S. with something other than regular criminal charges. For suspects abroad, the U.S. has used spies, drones and commandos to hunt down those accused of terrorism — to either kill them or drag them back to face charges in the U.S.

Why deport a terrorist? It’s a question that still confounds Alfred Wolin, 93, a retired federal judge who served on the ATRC for eight years and is the only jurist still alive of the five who were initially assigned to the special court in 1996.

“I don’t really know what the assignment was going to be in its totality,” he told NOTUS from his home in New Jersey. “And I'm not even sure to whom we would report.”

Wolin never met with his fellow ATRC judges. Plans to convene and discuss how the court would operate were scrapped. And he distinctly remembers being told by a high-ranking court official that the special tribunal never got any cases because “the FBI blocked any cases being sent to us.”

“I have no idea why,” Wolin said. “As far as I was concerned, it died.”

Last week, the DOJ revived it, filing its first application to the court — a process shrouded in mystery that doesn’t even include the name of the person it seeks to deport or why. Prosecutors with its National Security Division presented the case directly to Judge Joan Ericksen, a U.S. District judge in Minnesota who also serves as the ATRC’s chief judge.

The only public part of the July 15 application is a cover page that makes reference to the classified nature of the case, first reported by Court Watch. Prosecutors presented their arguments to Ericksen behind closed doors on July 16, and she responded with a follow-up order demanding more information.

“The court had questions about the nexus that the government alleges between the actions of the respondent and the specific sections and subsections it invokes with respect to those actions,” she wrote.

The judge gave prosecutors until this Wednesday to include additional “factual or legal analysis to satisfy its statutory obligations” in its application, but the court website didn’t show any additional public filings on Thursday morning.

Congress created the court with 1996’s Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act, a Republican-led pushback on the Clinton administration that limited death row appeals and made it easier to deport immigrants convicted of crimes. Then-Rep. Chuck Schumer (D-New York) called it a “better-than-nothing anti-terrorism bill” that he would “sadly and reluctantly” support. President Bill Clinton signed it into law.

Then-Sen. Bob Smith, a New Hampshire Republican, tucked the provision for a new, secret deportation court into the bill. Smith said it would be modeled after the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act court, which considers security agency requests for surveillance warrants against foreigners inside the United States.

Warning of a growing threat of terrorism, Smith envisioned a legal process that would allow prosecutors to withhold classified evidence from an immigrant accused of terrorism.

He also noted the bill was passed “in memory of the one-year anniversary of the Oklahoma City bombings,” despite the FBI calling it “the deadliest act of homegrown terrorism in U.S. history.” The bombing was planned and perpetrated by Timothy McVeigh, a U.S. Army veteran who joined the Ku Klux Klan and counted the racist book “The Turner Diaries” among his favorite literature.

“Far too often, deporting dangerous terrorists is complicated and difficult for our law enforcement officials. The bill we passed tonight would alleviate some of the problems with this process," Smith said in a press release at the time.

Smith is now a member of the Trump’s administration’s Homeland Security Advisory Council. He did not respond to a request for comment.

During congressional debate over the bill, then-Sen. Joe Biden criticized what he called “a secret hearing, using secret evidence.” He envisioned a defendant saying, “Hey, tell me who said I was a terrorist. How do you know that?” only to have the government respond, “Oh, no, we can’t tell you. We know you did it, and we can’t tell you how we know.”

Part of the new law was immediately used in the summer of 1996 to crack down on immigrants, with the Supreme Court ordering the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to reconsider its postponement of an Egyptian man’s deportation over selling $100 worth of hashish.

But the Clinton DOJ refused to file a terrorist deportation case in the special court, prompting then-Sen. Orrin Hatch to write to Vice President Al Gore later that year to complain that not “a single terrorist alien [has] been deported pursuant to the terrorist alien removal provisions.” The letter cited the Centennial Olympic Park bombing in Atlanta that summer, which investigators later found was carried out not by an immigrant but by U.S. citizen Eric Rudolph, an anti-abortion zealot.

Wolin, the retired judge, recalled how he got put on the new tribunal. It all started at the Greenbrier resort in West Virginia, where federal judges had gathered to mingle. Chief Justice William Rehnquist needed a tennis partner and asked Wolin to play with him against U.S. Judge H. Lee Sarokin of the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals and a second appellate judge in Pennsylvania.

“Rehnquist was not what I would call an accomplished tennis player,” Wolin remembered with a chuckle. “I think he was relying on me.”

A week or so after the game, the chief justice leaned on him again. A Supreme Court administrative assistant called Wolin, then a trial judge in New Jersey, to inform him that the chief justice wanted to appoint him to something called the Alien Terrorist Removal Court.

“It sounded like something I would be interested in doing, but we never received a case,” said Wolin, who still keeps a 2002 letter signed by Rehnquist in a plaque hanging on a wall in his basement.

Liam O’Grady, another retired federal judge who served on the special court from 2021 to 2023, said he never held any meetings with fellow judges on this assignment either. He said the current case’s true nature is anyone’s guess.

O’Grady acknowledged that it would make little sense for the U.S. government not to imprison a person deemed a true danger to the American public — unless, that is, some spy agency has concluded that convicting the person would require exposing sensitive information or espionage tactics in open court.

However, the U.S. justice system already has an established process for handling this kind of volatile evidence: the Classified Information Procedures Act of 1980, which allows defense lawyers with security clearances to build their cases while keeping their clients largely in the dark. This process has been used in cases against government employees accused of selling military secrets, foreign secret agents and even President Donald Trump when he was charged with retaining classified documents at Mar-a-Lago.

So why go this route for the first time in 30 years? O’Grady reasoned the DOJ might head to the Alien Terrorist Removal Court if the evidence is so sensitive that the government isn’t even willing to share it with a vetted defense lawyer — or expose vague summaries of it in open court. The ATRC permits the government to present evidence directly to a judge without the typical due process that allows a defendant to understand the nature of the charges against them.

According to a 2015 legal paper written by Jonathan H. Yu, then an adviser to DOJ immigration lawyers, lawful permanent residents accused in this special court get an extra layer of protection via a panel of vetted attorneys who may review the evidence in the judge’s chambers to “challenge the veracity of that classified information.”

A 2008 legal paper written by a Duke University law student noted that the court’s procedure “does not implicate the Sixth Amendment right to confront one’s accuser because ATRC proceedings are immigration rather than criminal proceedings” and the accused are non-citizens.

A provision in the law says the accused person doesn’t even have the right to challenge evidence that was illegally obtained.

American law professors David Cole and Stephen Vladeck decried these exceptions to widely accepted civil rights in an essay included in a 2014 legal compendium, “Reasoning Rights: Comparative Judicial Engagement.”

“The right to confront the evidence used to deprive a person of his liberty is essential to fundamental (and indeed, constitutional) notions of fairness,” Cole and Vladeck wrote.

They noted that Canada’s supreme court in 2007 rejected that government’s attempt to deport several men accused of Islamist extremism while relying on a secretive court and hidden evidence. (One of the men is an imam named Adil Charkaoui who would give a speech in 2023 calling for Allah to “kill the enemies of the people of Gaza,” which led to an investigation by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police but no criminal charges.)

The Canadian supreme court decision led the country to adopt a system in which defendants are still kept in the dark but third-party “cleared counsel” can see secret evidence and make legal challenges on their behalf.

That experience could serve as a warning as the United States begins to employ its secret deportation court for the first time.

O’Grady, who was a federal district judge in Virginia, suspects that the DOJ never filed a terrorist deportation case until now because “it's out of sight, out of mind, and it's never been used because no one knew how to use it.”

But he said he recognizes concerns over the Trump administration’s attempt to expand the definition of “terrorism” with two executive orders that aim to designate anti-fascists as a “domestic terrorist organization” and direct law enforcement to combat those who hold views considered to display “anti-Americanism,” “anti-capitalism” and “extremism on migration, race, and gender.”

“It's not an idle thought. This administration has looked for many different ways to aggressively respond to what it believes are big immigration problems, and they believe they have a mandate from the public to be aggressive,” O’Grady said. “So, are they curious as to whether this is another tool they can use? That may be part of the inspiration, but again, who knows. We're going to have to see what shakes out.”

entries.title: House Votes to Rein In Trump’s Iran War
entries.summary: Four Republicans voted for the measure.
entries.content:
The House voted Thursday to limit President Donald Trump’s authority to expand the war with Iran, its first war powers action since a temporary agreement with Tehran collapsed and fighting resumed.

The resolution, led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), passed 214-208. Four Republicans — Reps. Tom Barrett, Brian Fitzpatrick, Thomas Massie and Warren Davidson — joined Democrats as renewed fighting raised fears of a wider conflict.

“The president is once again showing his contempt for Congress and for the Constitution, continuing this destructive, deadly, and costly war despite Congress having already passed a War Powers Resolution that has the force of law,” Jayapal said Wednesday.

This was the House’s second vote to end the war. Like the first, which happened in early June, this vote cannot legally force Trump to stop the fighting. But the vote adds to signs of bipartisan concern over his decision to continue the war without congressional authorization as the conflict intensifies.

Four U.S. service members were killed in the latest escalation, bringing the American death toll to 18. More than 430 troops have been wounded since the war began. U.S. strikes against Iran have continued for 12 consecutive nights.

One of the Republican backers of the House war powers resolution, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, said the collapse of peace negotiations and the troop deaths might be driving GOP support. He said he has been supporting the resolutions to assert Congress’ powers over the executive branch.

“I follow the law,” Fitzpatrick said. “Under the War Powers Act of 1973, it says you’ve got to give a 48-hour notification, and after 60 days of hostilities, you’ve got to come to us” for authorization.

The administration says Trump has sufficient authority under the Constitution’s Article II to continue the campaign.

“We have all the authorities necessary at this moment,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday at a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing.

Trump told Congress in a July 10 letter that hostilities had resumed July 7 after the administration accused Tehran of violating a memorandum of understanding that had paused the fighting. The administration says the renewed campaign started a new 60-day period under the War Powers Resolution, a position lawmakers in both parties have questioned.

Republicans opposed to the resolution argued that limiting Trump during active hostilities would undermine U.S. forces and benefit Iran.

entries.title: Mark Sanford Jumps Into Crowded Race for Lindsey Graham’s Senate Seat
entries.summary: Graham’s sister is running. So are Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman.
entries.content:
Mark Sanford, the former congressman and governor of South Carolina, announced Thursday that he will run for the Senate seat held until recently by the late Lindsey Graham.

“Our country is at a financial tipping point, and I can't sit on the sidelines while Washington adds a trillion dollars to the debt every 100 days,” Sanford said in a post on X. “I've spent my entire time in politics fighting this fight, and I'm running for U.S. Senate to keep the American dream alive for our sons, my grandson, and those you love.”

The post was accompanied by a video of Sanford saying Graham’s death is a reminder of “how short and precious life is.”

Graham’s seat is temporarily being filled by his sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to serve out his term by Gov. Henry McMaster. She also announced this week that she would campaign for a full term, joining a crowded primary field that also includes Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman.

The primary is set for Aug. 11.

Sanford was South Carolina’s governor from 2003 to 2011, and he represented the 1st Congressional District twice, between 1995 and 2001 and between 2013 and 2019.

entries.title: The Senate Is Struggling to Pass Lindsey Graham’s Last Bill
entries.summary: Lawmakers are running out of time to pass a Russia sanctions bill before recess.
entries.content:
Supporters of a long-stalled Russian sanctions bill hoped it would gain momentum in the Senate after the sudden death of its top champion: Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Initially, at least, it seemed like the bill was on track to pass before the August recess. Graham, a South Carolina Republican, announced before his death that he had reached a deal with the White House to move forward. The bill surpassed 60 co-sponsors, giving it a filibuster-proof majority. Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her brother’s seat, also signed on, fueling optimism it would finally succeed.

Instead, the measure is once again at risk of stalling out.

“We're going to screw around here and lose this bill if we don't go vote,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told NOTUS. “We just pissed away two weeks. Now we got a week and a half left, and I don’t know if a vote is scheduled.”

Some Democrats are concerned the bill could harm U.S. allies. The White House has warned it wouldn’t have enough flexibility to waive sanctions. And President Donald Trump has demanded the bill include fresh sanctions on Iran, throwing another wrench into the carefully negotiated legislation.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday that he hopes to get the bill “teed up” next week. He said lawmakers were “homing in on” including Iran sanctions — which Darline Graham is championing.

But Thune has not yet secured an agreement from Democrats to fast-track the bill, which would need all 100 senators to agree.

Without that, it would take the Senate days to consider the bill under its arcane rules — time that Thune cannot spare given a laundry list of legislation and confirmations he wants to plow through before they leave Aug. 6, including Jay Clayton for director of national intelligence and Todd Blanche for attorney general.

The bill, titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026, would penalize countries that continue to import Russian oil and natural gas. The idea has been to choke off a revenue stream Russia uses to fund its war against Ukraine more than four years after its full-scale invasion.

The revamped bill more narrowly applies sanctions to the top five purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas while reducing the tariff from a blanket 500% to 100%. It would grant exceptions for countries weaning themselves off Russian supplies.

Some of the Democrats who haven’t signed onto the bill argue the tariff provisions are still too broad, however, and worry it would give Trump unprecedented power to sanction any country he sees fit, including European allies.

“Giving Trump additional authorities to act on tariffs in a reckless way that he's been doing is deeply concerning,” Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock said.

Vermont Sen. Peter Welch said the bill’s broad language “gives the executive carte blanche to do what he wants for whatever reason he wants.”

“That actually is in conflict with every conversation I had with Lindsey about how the tariffs should be targeted to achieve the specific goal of squeezing Russia's revenue,” Welch continued.

Backers of the revised Russia sanctions bill worked this week to maintain momentum.

One of the lead Democratic negotiators, New Hampshire Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, said she wasn’t opposed to adding Iran sanctions, noting they were in an earlier version of the bill and echo language Congress passed before.

“I’d like the Senate to add Iran back in to address the service members being killed by Iran, myself, but those discussions are still ongoing,” she said.

Lindsey Graham’s lead co-sponsor, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), said Darline Graham requested personally that Iran sanctions be included, so he is inclined to try. However, his preference is to proceed with the deal already reached with Trump.

Meanwhile, Blumenthal has been trying to tamp down concerns from both parties, including the Democrats who are worried about handing Trump more tariff authority.

“What we're finding is that some of those concerns are based on a fictional notion of the bill, without an understanding of the real constraints on Trump's authority under the bill,” he said.

Democrats are discussing tweaks to address the tariff provisions. But Blumenthal pushed back on suggestions that negotiators are preparing substantial revisions to win over skeptics.

“This bill was the result of very painstaking, often painful negotiations involving the U.S. trade representative, White House, colleagues and leadership,” he said. “My hope is it will be passed as-is. But I'm not the only one who has a say in this process. And my objective, first and foremost, is to get the bill to be law.”

With the August recess quickly approaching, the Senate is staring at the possibility of bungling its best chance yet to pass the bill. Failing to move ahead would deal a blow to Ukraine’s fight against Russia — and to Graham’s legacy.

“We should all remember the press conference we had on a bipartisan basis last week about remembering Graham's legacy,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said. “Anybody that says they'd oppose it because it doesn't go far enough — everything that we can drop, every straw we can drop on the camel's back for Putin counts, and we should pass it. That should be one thing that we get done.”

entries.title: White House Says It Won’t Intervene in Tate Brothers’ Extradition Process
entries.summary: Vice President JD Vance still follows both “manosphere” influencers on X, despite new allegations of rape and human trafficking.
entries.content:
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said on Thursday that the Trump administration would not intervene in the extradition process of the controversial “manosphere” influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate.

The Tate brothers, who were first formally indicted in Romania on charges of human trafficking and organized crime in 2023, were arrested by U.S. Marshals in Florida last week following an extradition request from the United Kingdom in connection with new criminal charges of rape and sex trafficking in the country.

Though both siblings deny any wrongdoing, at the beginning of the month the British government brought additional charges against the two, including seven more counts of rape and child pornography against Andrew, and two more counts of rape against Tristan; both face counts of sexual assault and sex trafficking.

Self-proclaimed “misogynist” Andrew Tate is a prominent voice in the manosphere — a loose-knit group of male internet personalities — and popular in some MAGA circles. Some of his supporters include Donald Trump Jr., who has publicly defended Tate, and Richard Grenell, a longtime Trump ally who serves as a special presidential envoy.

But when asked whether the president or any of his top officials would step in to assist the pair, Leavitt answered emphatically.

“No. We've already answered that question,” Leavitt said.

As of Thursday, Vice President JD Vance still follows both brothers on X. 

The Trump administration reportedly raised concerns with Romanian officials in 2025 over the travel restrictions placed on the brothers while a separate criminal case remained ongoing. President Donald Trump denied any personal involvement in the matter.

entries.title: Private Prison Employee Accused of Shooting of Anti-ICE Protester in Colorado
entries.summary: Brandon Booth fired a shot between two protestors, hitting one, after they were involved in a verbal altercation, according to local police.
entries.content:
An individual working for a private prison contractor has been charged in connection with a shooting that injured a protester outside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Colorado, prosecutors announced Wednesday.

District Attorney Brian Mason charged Brandon Booth, who is currently on administrative leave from detention center operator GEO Group, with assault and attempted assault. Booth allegedly discharged his personally owned weapon on July 16 near protesters outside an ICE facility in Aurora, Colorado, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by local media including news station Denver7.

Aurora police said Booth fired a round between two demonstrators and hit one, Emma Landis, in the foot. Booth left the scene in his vehicle but was apprehended by police, who said in the affidavit that Booth realized the incident had been caught on cameras and that he had “done some dumb shit.”

Booth said was attempting to scare the protestors, who were blocking employees from entering, according to CBS News.

He told police that as Landis and the other demonstrator walked by, they said, "We got your license plate, we're gonna run you down, we're gonna have people at your kids' school." Booth said his anger grew to "a 15 out of 10," after hearing the comment.

Several days after receiving medical treatment for her injuries, Landis returned to the ongoing protest outside of the ICE facility, Colorado Public Radio reported.

“I will continue to advocate for this stuff,” she said in an interview with More Perfect Union. “I got shot for it. I care.”

The incident in Aurora follows a pair of fatal shootings in Texas and Maine by federal immigration agents. In both shootings, the individuals were killed in their vehicles.

Booth is facing two felonies, with the assault charge carrying a sentence of 10 to 32 years in prison under Colorado law.

GEO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NOTUS, but a spokesperson told NBC News on Friday that Booth had been placed on unpaid administrative leave.

Booth’s next court date is scheduled for Aug. 13.

entries.title: Boosie Badazz’s Estranged MAGA Lobbyists Just Inked a New Trump Pardon Client
entries.summary: The rapper has accused Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl of reneging on a promise to return $300,000 if they did not quickly secure a pardon.
entries.content:
Another criminal who wants President Donald Trump to pardon him for his financial crimes has hired Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl — two convicted fraudsters who are facing legal action from rapper Boosie Badazz, a former pardon client who’s accused the duo of misleading him.

Burkman and Wohl registered last week to lobby on behalf of Rajendra Parikh, who was sentenced last month to two years in prison for his role in a multimillion-dollar fraud scheme. Judge Deborah Chasanow also ordered Parikh, who pleaded guilty in 2025 to conspiracy to commit bank fraud, to forfeit $6 million and pay more than $6 million in restitution.

Neither Burkman nor Parikh’s lawyer, Robert Welsh, responded to requests for comment.

Burkman and Wohl have signed several clients seeking federal pardons or support on “DOJ issues” since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. One of their clients, the nursing home mogul Joseph Schwartz, secured a pardon last fall.

But as NOTUS reported last week, Boosie, whose legal name is Torence Hatch, is taking legal action against Burkman, Wohl and the firm.
BoosieBadazz.1 (4928x3280, AR: 1.50)Boosie, who has not received a pardon and terminated his contract with the firm in March, has accused Burkman and Wohl of withholding half of the $600,000 retainer that the rapper said they agreed to repay if they did not quickly secure a federal pardon, according to a copy of the signed contract reviewed by NOTUS.

JM Burkman & Associates previously said in a statement to NOTUS that “no provision to return half the fee was ever actually agreed to.” In text messages reviewed by NOTUS, Burkman told Boosie in March that he and Wohl were “essentially bankrupt.”

Burkman and Wohl owe millions of dollars in fines for running an illegal robocall scheme that targeted Black voters in several states, urging them to avoid voting by mail.

The pair pleaded guilty to telecommunications fraud in Ohio in 2022 and are required to disclose the felony convictions on their federal lobbying registrations and reports. They later pleaded no contest in Michigan and agreed to pay $1.25 million to settle the case in New York, and the Federal Communications Commission fined them more than $5 million.

Wohl also claimed in text messages reviewed by NOTUS that prominent MAGA influencers and politicians had endorsed Boosie’s pardon, but several told NOTUS or said after publication that they knew nothing about the matter.

“No offense but I also have no idea who you are and have never heard of your case. Seems like Burkman is using people’s names without permission to get business,” Laura Loomer wrote on X in response to a post from Boosie asking if she and others had spoken with the lobbyists about his pardon request.

JM Burkman & Associates previously told NOTUS that it “cannot think of a single client for whom our firm has done more work than Boosie.”

Burkman and Wohl started lobbying for Parikh on July 14, one day after NOTUS reported on the fallout between Boosie and his former pardon lobbyists. By law, Burkman and Wohl do not have to disclose until mid-October how much Parikh is paying them.

JM Burkman & Associates’ federal lobbying revenue has skyrocketed since the start of Trump’s second term, and their work is not limited to pardon lobbying. The firm reported $3.2 million in revenue in 2025, up from $1.6 million in 2024, according to federal lobbying data analyzed by OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan nonprofit that tracks the flow of money in politics.

The firm has reported making $1.4 million during the first six months of 2026, including $770,000 between April and June, according to a NOTUS analysis of federal lobbying disclosures.
