entries.title: Rep. Dan Crenshaw Violated the STOCK Act — Again
entries.summary: The Texas Republican failed to properly disclose personal stock trades as the House moved to ban lawmakers’ trades altogether.
entries.content:
Rep. Dan Crenshaw has again violated a federal insider trading and transparency law by failing to properly disclose a pair of personal stock-option trades, according to new congressional financial filings reviewed by NOTUS.

Crenshaw, a Texas Republican, purchased up to $15,000 worth of stock options in Meta, the parent company of Facebook, on April 28. He then sold an equal number of Meta stock options at a higher price point on May 5, the financial filing indicates.

In both cases, Crenshaw publicly disclosed his stock-option purchases about a month past a 45-day federal deadline mandated by the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act, which lawmakers have regularly violated since Congress passed it in 2012. The law, meant to defend against lawmaker insider trading and conflicts of interest, only carries a $200 initial fine for violations, which the House and Senate ethics committees may waive at their discretion.

It’s unclear precisely how much money Crenshaw, who earlier this year lost his reelection bid in a Republican primary, earned from the transactions.

Crenshaw made disclosures this week of other personal stock purchases, including shares of Apple, Amazon, Alphabet and the United States 3x Oil Fund, a now-delisted exchange-traded fund that aims to triple the performance of light, sweet crude oil futures. These purchases were disclosed within the deadline mandated by law.

Crenshaw sits on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, whose jurisdiction includes energy policy and telecommunications.Crenshaw’s chief of staff, Jerome Vainisi, told NOTUS that “Rep. Crenshaw has no comment to offer on this story.”

Crenshaw’s STOCK Act violations come the same week the U.S. House passed the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would ban members of Congress trading individual stocks, although it would allow them to retain existing stock holdings.

Crenshaw voted in favor of the Republican-backed bill, which also attracted 13 Democratic votes to advance the measure by 232-198. The bill’s prospects in the Senate, however, appear bleak.

This is also not the first time Crenshaw violated the STOCK Act. He failed to properly report several personal stock moves in early 2020, including trades of Amazon, Southwest Airlines and Boeing.

“Any reporting issues were unintentional and are being corrected immediately,” Crenshaw told the Houston Chronicle after The Daily Beast first reported on the matter.

Rep. Laurel Lee (R-Florida) also appears to have violated the STOCK Act’s disclosure rules. This week, she reported her husband’s sale of up to $50,000 in Nokia stock shares a couple weeks after the STOCK Act’s reporting deadline.

Lee’s congressional office acknowledged an inquiry from NOTUS but did not respond to questions.

Crenshaw and Lee join a roster of other members of Congress who in the past year have violated the STOCK Act with improperly disclosed financial trades.

They include then-Sen. Markwayne Mullin (R-Oklahoma) and Sens. Katie Britt (R-Alabama), Susan Collins (R-Maine), John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado), Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) and John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania).

In the House, STOCK Act violators include Reps. Linda Sánchez (D-California), Julia Letlow (R-Louisiana), Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Lisa McClain (R-Michigan), Pat Ryan (D-New York), Sheri Biggs (R-South Carolina), Donald Norcross (D-New Jersey), Tim Walberg (R-Michigan), Rich McCormick (R-Georgia), Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Troy Nehls (R-Texas), Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois), George Whitesides (D-California), Val Hoyle (D-Oregon), Austin Scott (R-Georgia), Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Florida), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), Kelly Morrison (D-Minnesota), Christian Menefee (D-Texas), Daniel Webster (R-Florida), Ed Case (D-Hawaii) and Scott Franklin (R-Florida). Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma) was also late, although his office denies it.

entries.title: Hegseth Picks New DOD University Partners After Dumping Ivy League Schools
entries.summary: UNC-Chapel Hill and Virginia Tech are the first universities selected after the Pentagon cut ties with several elite schools.
entries.content:
The Defense Department this week announced the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and Virginia Tech as the newest hosts of a reworked educational program for service members, a decision that came after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth cut ties with several Ivy League institutions.

The two universities were the first to be selected by the department and will soon offer the Senior Service College Fellowship, a 10-month professional program for senior military officers.

“We are deeply honored to participate,” UNC-Chapel Hill Chancellor Lee H. Roberts said in a statement. “The program fits well within the context of our mission of service, and we take tremendous pride in our deep, longstanding relationship with the United States military.”

Earlier this year, Hegseth announced the Defense Department had canceled the fellowship program at several Ivy League schools, including Columbia University, Harvard University and Yale University — institutions that had historically offered the program for military members.

Under his leadership, Hegseth said the department had realigned its academic partnerships to better reflect the administration’s goals.

In a social media post in February, the secretary argued the elite schools had become the grounds for “woke indoctrination” and that the universities fomented “anti-American resentment and military disdain.” The Pentagon has canceled at least 93 fellowship programs and cut ties with 13 higher education institutions.

Hegseth's decision to end fellowships that sent senior military officers to select U.S. universities has sparked confusion within the armed services and concerns that officers will lose access to some of the nation's top academic institutions, NOTUS previously reported. 

More universities are expected to join the new cohort in the coming weeks. In a memo, the department suggested several conservative-leaning schools, such as Hillsdale College, Liberty University and the University of Florida, as likely partners.

entries.title: Democrats See an Opening on Trade — If They Can Agree
entries.summary: Democrats see the Trump administration’s renegotiations of USMCA as a political opportunity.
entries.content:
Democrats say they have an opportunity to stand up to President Donald Trump on trade. They just haven't reached a consensus on what their trade agenda is.

The Trump administration opened the door to a renegotiation of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. In a hearing with senators this week, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he wanted interim agreements with both countries by the end of the year, and to tackle thornier issues in 2027.

Those talks, according to Rep. Jimmy Panetta (D-California), are Democrats’ chance to “take back trade” from Republicans, who he says have conceded to the president’s aggressive tariff regime. 

But Democrats, he said, need to get to work smoothing out their policy differences.

“The consensus isn't developed yet,” Panetta said. “But I think now more than ever we should be.”

Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, led a letter to Trump in November advocating for “significant renegotiations,” primarily to address Mexican wage issues, create new labor and environmental protections and enforce existing ones. That letter was signed by 104 other House Democrats.

Panetta was not one of them. The New Democrat Coalition wrote a letter, led by Panetta, last November advocating for more of a fine-tuning of the agreement. Only a handful of Democrats like Reps. Darren Soto (D-Florida), Tom Suozzi (D-New York) and Steven Horsford (D-Nevada) signed both letters.

“I would say 90% of the congressional Democrats, House and Senate, have a particular position, which is pretty much reflected in DeLauro’s letter, which lays out at a high level the whole kit and the caboodle,” Lori Wallach, director of the Rethink Trade program and an expert on congressional trade battles, told NOTUS. “However, there are outliers.”

These are the big-picture ideas Democrats agree on: they don’t want to exit the deal entirely as Trump has threatened to, they want certainty for businesses and, broadly, they want to strengthen labor and environmental protections.

The disagreements come down to the specifics. For example, DeLauro called for stronger rules of origin — the guidelines that specify a product’s nationality — whereas Rep. Linda Sánchez of California, the top Democrat on the Ways and Means trade subcommittee, instead argued that existing rules just needed clarification.

DeLauro’s letter panned USMCA as a failure that offshored U.S. manufacturing jobs. The New Democrats’ letter makes no mention of offshoring, and the coalition called the trade agreement a “cornerstone of North American competitiveness” in a letter Monday.

Rep. Val Hoyle (D-Oregon) said her Democratic colleagues who supported the North American Free Trade Agreement, which USMCA replaced, are engaging in talks on strategically deploying tariffs to protect American jobs from offshoring.

“What we have seen in Mexico is that wages are lower, environmental standards are not the same as we have here, and it's not fair that we offshore issues like underpayment of workers or environmental degradation to another country. We can't be blind to that,” Hoyle said.

“They are open to that conversation, and I'm talking to people who come from very, very different places on what tariffs should be, and I feel like we're in a really good place,” she added.

As they find their footing, multiple Democrats signaled frustration over communication between the Trump administration and Congress on USMCA.

“I’ve been surprised that there has not been consultation,” Rep. Richard Neal (D-Massachusetts) told NOTUS last week of the White House’s communication with Congress.

Democrats said there’s been a more open line of communication with Greer. DeLauro told NOTUS that she and others met with Greer recently to discuss their interests.

So far, Democrats’ efforts to exert influence over USMCA have been limited to letters and statements, hampered by the fact that they are in the minority. But they could find themselves in a position of real leverage and influence should they take the House in the midterms.

After Democrats won back the House in 2018, the new majority forced the Trump administration to redo USMCA negotiations to secure members’ votes. Unlike in 2019, however, approval from Congress is not required unless the Trump administration negotiates changes to the USMCA that are significant enough to require legislation to be changed or updated. Already the administration has signaled it does not want the agreement to go to Congress.

“If Dems take back the House they, have substantial oversight capabilities, which is a really important tool to drive the narrative through hearings and engaging with the administration,” said Allison Smith, a vice president at communications and lobbying firm Lot Sixteen and a former deputy assistant U.S. trade representative.

Democrats are prioritizing trade on the campaign trail. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee cited tariffs as one of Republicans’ biggest vulnerabilities heading into the crucial elections.

In the interim, Panetta and DeLauro told NOTUS they think the differences are surmountable.

“We voted for it the first time around. Now we're talking about what are the changes that need to be made, and you know where we are on digital trade, wages and offshoring. You know, the environmental piece,” she said. “The rapid-response mechanisms work, but it's got to be better. We’ve got to focus on making the agreement more worker-centric.”

“I think the discussions are beginning. I think we can come out in the same place.”

Panetta, however, did raise another possible complication. Some congressional Democrats are just not up to speed on the issue.

“There are different levels of understanding of trade by different levels of members,” Panetta told NOTUS. “There are members who aren't really as on trade, yet they're politically driven rather than policy driven.”

entries.title: McConnell’s Absence is Grinding Some Senate Business to a Halt
entries.summary: Farm bill and government funding negotiations are at a standstill without Sen. Mitch McConnell, with just 10 legislative weeks left this year.
entries.content:
Sen. Mitch McConnell’s extended absence has thrown a number of the Senate’s top priorities into limbo.

McConnell has not voted since he was hospitalized following a fall on June 14, and it’s still unclear when the Kentucky Republican will return to the upper chamber. His absence has complicated the math for leadership on several key votes as Republicans continue to grapple with a slim majority and only 10 legislative weeks before the end of the year.

“We’re at 52” Republican votes, Majority Leader John Thune told NOTUS, versus the 53 seats the party holds in the Senate. “This is the reality.”

McConnell’s absence is a particular problem for committees trying to negotiate urgent matters such as government funding and the farm bill.

The Appropriations Committee has been at a standstill for about a month on talks to avoid a government shutdown. Without McConnell, who chairs the subcommittee on defense, the Appropriations Committee is split 14-14 between Democrats and Republicans, making it impossible to advance legislation that doesn’t have bipartisan support.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), who serves on the committee, told NOTUS that losing McConnell’s vote in such partisan negotiations has made those conversations “impossible.”

“We miss not just his vote, we miss him,” Capito said. “But it definitely has an impact on approps –– it’s probably the most deeply felt.”

Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins said she’s hopeful that McConnell will return before the committee has to vote on any kind of funding bill.

“I believe he will be back in September, so I am very optimistic about that,” said Collins, a Republican from Maine.

Talks over the farm bill are also at a standstill without McConnell, the second-ranking Republican on the Agriculture Committee. Democrats want to delay when states must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, a provision that Republicans are staunchly opposed to.

McConnell’s absence leaves the committee at 11-11, giving Democrats a new leg up in those negotiations. Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) told NOTUS that every day the bill is delayed is difficult for farmers in his home state.

“Let’s just pray that he gets back really, really soon and gets back in a good, healthy way where we can move this along,” Justice said.

Justice said Congress should pass a bill to prevent these sorts of absences from causing legislative impasses in the future. He suggested that if a lawmaker’s absence stretched beyond 30 days, their party could be allowed to select someone to fill their place on committees.

“That completely is so reasonable it’s unbelievable to me,” Justice said.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) told NOTUS that repeated Republican absences are causing consistent problems for committee work and other legislative business in the upper chamber.

“Basically, we’ve been unable to do stuff today in committees,” Hawley said. “All the committees I was in today had to be canceled or couldn’t do business because Republicans weren’t there. And I’m like, wow, we’ve got two weeks to go.”

Hawley added that the issue extends to the Senate floor. On Thursday, Senate Republicans shot down a resolution limiting the Trump administration’s war powers in Iran, but any absence can make those kinds of votes all the more difficult.

“There’s only 53 votes,” Hawley said. “When you have multiple people gone at a time, it's like, well, you can't even control the floor. It’s got to be frustrating to be the leader.”

But other Senate Republicans said they aren’t taking issue with McConnell’s extended absence just yet. Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska) noted that other senators have also taken time off from legislating for medical reasons.

Fischer pointed to former Sen. Mark Kirk (R-Illinois), who was absent for a full year after suffering a stroke in 2012, and former Sen. Tim Johnson (D-South Dakota), who missed nine months after a brain hemorrhage in 2006.

“I would say there wasn't the deep interest that Sen. McConnell has been under,” Fischer said of those previous absences. “He's doing some rehabilitation. He wants to come back, that's his choice.”

Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said simply: “I have not missed a vote since I've been here. … I just can only control myself.”

entries.title: Staffing Cuts Are Threatening NASA’s Plan to Land on the Moon
entries.summary: The space agency “may not be able to staff all planned work” going forward, auditor finds.
entries.content:
Workforce cuts are putting NASA’s plans to send astronauts to the moon and, eventually, Mars, at risk, according to a new audit from the government’s top watchdog.

NASA shed 4,000 of its permanent staff last year, an overhaul officials said is now impacting 70% of its major projects. The agency has felt the cuts throughout its headquarters and in each of its centers across the country, the Government Accountability Office found in a report released on Thursday.

The Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland was the hardest hit, shedding more than one-third of its workforce through a hiring freeze and various separation incentives, followed by the Langley Research Center in Virginia and the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The Jet Propulsion Laboratory, operated by the California Institute of Technology, also laid off 10% of its workforce.

“The civil servant departures have left NASA’s workforce out of balance with NASA’s programmatic needs,” GAO said.

Staff working on 25 of NASA’s 36 major projects told the watchdog they were suffering ill effects from the workforce cuts.

The Space Launch System, the vehicle for launching the Artemis missions, lost 20% of its civilian workforce. The program is still analyzing the impacts of those losses but considers staffing issues as a possible risk to future Artemis missions. Artemis II sent four crew members around the moon earlier this year. Artemis III is set to serve as another test run next year before Artemis IV’s planned landing on the moon in 2028.

The Orion program, which provides the spacecraft used by the Artemis missions, shed 10% of its civil servants and has struggled to backfill “key positions.” Projects related to Artemis reported technical and programmatic risks that “were likely to delay their schedules” going forward, GAO said.

Layoffs at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory hit both leadership and “hands-on hardware” development staff in the Near Earth Object Surveyor project, a planned infrared space telescope that will detect asteroids and comets that threaten Earth. A program designed to study Venus’ atmosphere lost so many program managers and engineers that it canceled various risk-reduction activities last year, but it has since sought to restore staffing.

Most of NASA’s major projects still made it through 2025 without significant schedule delays or cost overruns, GAO found, though more challenges may be on the horizon.

“Moving forward, some centers may be challenged to meet the workforce needs of the mission directorates because of the reduced civil servant workforce,” GAO said. “Some centers, particularly those that encountered large workforce losses, may not be able to adequately staff all planned work.”

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, a billionaire businessman and pilot who previously led several SpaceX missions, has put NASA on a different trajectory since taking office in December. He announced earlier this year that the agency would resume hiring after an extended freeze and address skill gaps.

The agency recently launched NASA Force with the Office of Personnel Management to recruit technical employees to key roles in two-year stints, which could be converted to permanent roles.

OPM Director Scott Kupor recently told NOTUS that NASA would look to fill many roles that had been outsourced to contractors with government staff.

In response to its report, Isaacman told GAO that NASA encountered “many challenges” in 2025, including the “departure of over 4,000 civil servants.”

“I commend the NASA workforce advancing the major programs and projects included in this year’s assessment — people who were able to adjust and respond in creative ways to continue their missions,” Isaacman said.

The administrator’s push to restaff the space agency could run into further resistance if the Trump administration has its way: The president’s fiscal 2027 budget proposed slashing NASA’s budget by 23%. President Donald Trump similarly suggested a $6 billion, or 24%, funding cut, the elimination of 19 projects and a 32% workforce reduction in fiscal 2026, though Congress largely ignored those proposals and kept the agency flat funded.

entries.title: Vance Secret Service Agent Investigated After Alleged Media Leak
entries.summary: The unidentified agent is facing “an administrative investigation, and potential criminal inquiry,” according to the agency.
entries.content:
A Secret Service agent on Vice President JD Vance’s detail is under investigation and faces potential criminal charges after private information was apparently leaked to the media.

The agent, who was not identified, “is the subject of an administrative investigation, and potential criminal inquiry, involving allegations of compromising operational and information security,” Secret Service spokesperson Anthony Guglielmi told NOTUS in a statement.

MS NOW reported last week that Vance’s security team was “fed up” with the vice president's personal travel schedule and said some agents considered their assignments to be inappropriate and burdensome. The story included details about Vance’s schedule that were not publicly known, and the Secret Service agent who is under investigation is accused of being a source for the article, according to CNN, which first reported the probe.

The Secret Service did not release any additional information about the matter.

“One principle is unequivocal: any conduct that potentially threatens the safety of a protectee will not be tolerated,” Guglielmi said.

The vice president’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

President Donald Trump’s administration has cracked down on federal officials’ communications with the news media in an effort to prevent leaks of government information.

The Office of Personnel Management proposed a new rule in May to apply sweeping nondisclosure agreements across the federal workforce. Government employees within the Defense Department and other national security-focused agencies were already subject to the agreements.

The Justice Department also issued subpoenas to four New York Times reporters over their reporting on security concerns regarding the new aircraft being used as Air Force One. The Qatari government gifted the Boeing 747-8 to the U.S. government in May 2025, and it was retrofitted to serve as the presidential aircraft.

entries.title: Minnesota Man Sentenced to Life in Prison for Killing Democratic Lawmaker Melissa Hortman
entries.summary: Vance Boelter was sentenced to two consecutive life terms after pleading guilty to a politically motivated attack that killed two and wounded two others.
entries.content:
Vance Boelter, a Minnesota man who shot and killed former state House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband in a politically motivated attack, was sentenced to life in prison on Thursday.

The 59-year-old man pleaded guilty in June to six federal charges, including the killings of Hortman and her husband, Mark, and the shootings of state Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette Hoffman, who were wounded but survived. His sentencing came more than a year after he stalked the Democratic lawmakers’ homes while pretending to be a law enforcement officer.

The judge from the bench said the sentence was “well-deserved.”

At Thursday’s hearing, relatives of the victims spoke about the attack’s enduring consequences, while federal prosecutors characterized Boelter’s actions as politically motivated violence aimed at elected officials. Boelter offered an apology in court before being sentenced to two consecutive life terms and an additional 40 years behind bars under the terms of his plea agreement.

The federal sentence does not resolve all the charges against Boelter. He continues to face a separate state prosecution in Minnesota, where he is charged with two counts of first-degree premeditated murder, four counts of attempted first-degree murder, impersonating a police officer and animal cruelty. The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office has indicated it intends to move forward with that case.

Federal prosecutors announced in June they will not seek the death penalty following Boelter’s plea that month.

"Bringing justice to the families and loved ones of victims of violence is the number one priority of the Department of Justice," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement last month. "Prosecutors worked hard on this case to make sure he was held accountable to the fullest extent possible."

entries.title: States Sue to Stop Trump Administration Effort to Control Elections
entries.summary: The Trump administration has threatened to withhold federal emergency disaster preparation funding from states that don’t comply with new election rules.
entries.content:
Twenty-five states and Washington, D.C., are suing the Trump administration for trying to use federal emergency grant funding to control state election rules.

The Department of Homeland Security has threatened to withhold 20% of Federal Emergency Management Agency homeland security funding from any state that doesn’t adopt strict new election procedures preferred by President Donald Trump.

Those rules from DHS include using hand-marked paper ballots instead of machines, the implementation of the SAVE database to search for registered voters who could be noncitizens, and handing the federal government information about state voter rolls.

“The conditions DHS is trying to impose would require states to make sweeping changes to the way we conduct elections, including rewriting state election laws and privacy laws,” Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul said in a news conference with the attorneys generals for Rhode Island, California and New Jersey, the four states leading the lawsuit.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Rhode Island, asks a judge to block implementation of the conditions, arguing in part that DHS overstepped Congress’ role and violated the regulatory process.

State coalitions have already twice sued the Trump administration over its attempts to withhold FEMA disaster funding from states that do not cooperate with new Trump administration immigration policies. In both cases, courts granted summary judgment to the states and forced the release of funds.

“I am disappointed, but not necessarily surprised, that our coalition is filing its third lawsuit today to protect this funding,” Raoul said.

DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

States, not the federal government, have central authority over their election rules. Imposing requirements on the distribution of federal disaster preparation funding is the latest strategy from the Trump administration to try to get around that limitation. Many states rely heavily on FEMA’s Homeland Security Grant Program to invest in law enforcement and plan for and protect against terrorist threats.

The SAVE database was originally created by DHS to check the citizenship status of people applying for government benefit programs.

But since 2024, Republicans in Congress have been trying to pass versions of the SAVE Act, the most recent iteration of which would force states to use the database to cut people from their voter rolls. The 2026 version of the bill is currently stalled in the Senate.

Election experts have repeatedly warned that implementing the SAVE database for voter roll checks could lead to accidentally disenfranchising people who are eligible to vote.

With the legislation stalled in Congress, DHS is instead trying to use grant funding to force states to implement SAVE.

“We’re back in court to ensure that these funds are distributed as Congress intended, not conditioned on an unlawful political agenda,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in the news conference. “Public safety should never become a bargaining chip.”

entries.title: John Thune and the White House Are Openly Fighting Over the SAVE Act
entries.summary: “John’s doing the best he can, but John can’t put a gun to people’s head and make them vote a particular way,” Sen. John Kennedy said.
entries.content:
The battle over the SAVE America Act ratcheted up a few notches Thursday as the White House and Senate Majority Leader John Thune traded barbs over the lack of progress on the voting bill that President Donald Trump considers his top priority.

Trump’s frustrations about the stalled legislation have simmered for months but took a sharp turn Wednesday. At a rally in Georgia, he panned the upper chamber as “a place you send things when you want them to die.”

But it was a back-and-forth between White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Thune that really added gas to the fire. When Leavitt was pressed about the Republican leader, she told reporters that the president's “patience is running out” — comments that did not sit well with Thune.

“She or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right?” the mild-mannered Thune shot back. “So instead of pointing the finger at Republicans, they might think about going after the people who are stopping it on the floor, which is the Democrats. And if there are Republicans that they think are gettable, get on the phone. Let’s get them to ‘yes.’”

The exchange marked the latest crescendo in a battle that has lasted for much of the year, with Trump loyalists pounding the table to get the bill to the president’s desk despite the fact it can’t pass the Senate.

The measure not only doesn’t have Democratic support to overcome a filibuster, it does not have the needed votes to weaken the 60-vote threshold in favor of a “talking” filibuster that Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) has championed. Even if that did happen, the bill has previously failed to win simple majority support.

“We just don’t have the votes, and so there’s nothing that Senator Thune can do to change that. This idea that he can just command members of the Republican Conference to get in line is just a fantasy, so I think it’s unfair,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) told reporters.

Thune is left taking the intra-party arrows every time he admits there is little that can be done to move the bill along. Republicans are left frustrated over what they believe are unrealistic expectations by Trump and conservative activists over the bill’s future.

Cornyn blamed people misleading the White House.

“I don’t know who it was that sold the president on this idea that this was attainable, but it’s creating a circular firing squad for Republicans,” Cornyn said. “Here we are, what, 103 days before the midterm elections, and this is not a great place for us to be.”

The bill would require voters to present a photo ID to vote and proof of citizenship for voter registration, and would severely curtail the use of mail-in balloting.

Trump has insisted that as much of the SAVE America Act as possible has to advance before the August recess. The House took a step of its own before it departed for a weekslong recess by green-lighting $10 billion in incentives for states to pass portions of the voting measure.

However, the Senate isn’t in lockstep.

Thune announced this week that he won’t move the House’s budget resolution before the August break. He explained this was a strategy to preserve a third reconciliation bill if one is needed to pass a government spending measure before the Sept. 30 funding deadline. He has also been loathe to allow another vote-a-rama, required under reconciliation rules, before November to keep from exposing vulnerable incumbents to tough votes.

A number of other Republicans also took issue with Leavitt’s characterization of Thune and indicated they believed he was dealing with the math.

“Everybody wants to talk about 60 votes — we don’t have 51 votes,” Sen. John Hoeven (R-North Dakota) said.

Others believe Thune has few options at his disposal.

“I don’t think it’s a news flash. John’s doing the best he can, but John can’t put a gun to people’s head and make them vote a particular way,” said Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana). “When you’re majority leader, you take a lot of the spears and the arrows. That’s his job.”

“I think John is generally for the [SAVE America Act.] It’s just that we have some people that aren’t,” he continued. Republican Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Thom TIllis of North Carolina and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska have voted against versions of the voting bill.

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Florida), who has at times been a thorn in Thune’s side and has been a preeminent supporter of the measure, indicated he’s sympathetic to both sides in the spat.

“It’s hard being leader. … I think he’s working hard,” Scott said of Thune. “I’m sure if I was the president of the United States, I’d be frustrated if everything I wanted didn’t get done. So that is probably pretty common.”

Trump has recently attempted to use the voting proposal as a cudgel, further complicating matters for the Republican leader. Last month he said he wouldn’t sign a reauthorization of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act unless SAVE America was approved as well.

At this point, Trump’s maneuvers have left members exasperated as they readily acknowledge the situation is basically at an impasse.

“Nobody said it was going to be easy,” Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) said about the bill before criticizing Leavitt’s remarks. “I can’t imagine that she knows what it’s like to be a leader in the Senate with 53 very strong-minded people that have different opinions.”

“If [the president’s] going to be an immovable force, I don’t know why they can’t be an immovable force too,” she said of Republicans opposing the SAVE America Act. “That’s what we’re seeing here — immovable forces coming up against one another.”

entries.title: DOJ Agrees to Withdraw Subpoenas Issued to New York Times Reporters
entries.summary: Government admits “mistakes” in probe of sources for articles about Air Force One security concerns.
entries.content:
NEW YORK — The Justice Department agreed Thursday to withdraw an attempt to force New York Times reporters to reveal to a grand jury their sources for a story on national security concerns about the Qatari-gifted airplane to replace Air Force One.

After rapid-fire questions from an upset judge and a mention of potential sanctions against prosecutors for the Justice Department, the government admitted to making several “mistakes” when launching an investigation that targeted journalists with subpoenas.

During an hourlong court hearing, U.S. District Judge Arun Subramanian grilled one of the highest-ranking prosecutors at the Southern District of New York over the DOJ’s ongoing attempt to identify the sources behind Times articles that revealed that security concerns prevented President Donald Trump from using his new airplane on a return trip from Turkey earlier this month.

Prosecutors told the judge that acting Attorney General Todd Blanche personally signed off on subpoenas that sought to force Times reporters Julian E. Barnes, Eric Lipton, Eric Schmitt, Tyler Pager and Adam Goldman to reveal the identities of the government officials who spoke to them.

Lawyers for the Times sought to quash those subpoenas.

Sean Buckley, a longtime SDNY prosecutor who is currently listed as the chief counsel to the U.S. attorney in that office, remained defensive as he stood to answer a barrage of questions from the judge.

Buckley said he oversaw the investigation and knew about the established restrictions limiting the government’s ability to pressure journalists to give up their sources, but that “those additional steps were not yet identified” by prosecutors before they pursued subpoenas.

“No one was looking to pull a fast one on the courts or anyone else,” he told the judge.

Subramanian asked a series of questions about the way the government sent FBI agents to reporters homes on July 10 to serve subpoenas compelling them to testify before a grand jury — and later tried to order communication service providers to fork over records of the reporter’s phone exchanges.

The backdrop to his questions is decades of government attempts to spy on journalists that resulted in First Amendment legal protections — in the form of official DOJ internal policies and case law — that demand prior authorization from DOJ brass and an investigation involving immediate risk to human lives.

The DOJ is also limited in its ability to force companies to keep silent about government attempts to acquire records of their customers’ private communications if the target is a reporter engaged in their constitutionally protected right to free speech.

Subramanian repeatedly asked Buckley if the government would be willing to simply withdraw the subpoenas. For the first hour, the prosecutor wouldn’t budge.

Subramanian quickly brought up how prosecutors, in court filings earlier this week, said they at first had not alerted lawyers for the journalists about subpoenas to third parties for phone numbers. The revelation came in a letter on Monday in which prosecutors cited “additional case law that the government identified after the issuance of the subpoenas.”

“Doesn’t that mean you failed the Gonzalez test?” the judge asked, referring to the appellate case that created that requirement.

“Those additional steps were not yet identified,” Buckley responded.

“Why doesn’t that mean that the motion to quash is granted?” the judge replied, shaking his head.

Subramanian remained focused on what he described as the government’s failure to properly investigate a matter before threatening journalists with jail time if they didn’t reveal their sources. The judge stressed that prosecutors were bound by a responsibility to investigate the matter before resorting to a drastic measure that would implicate “the profound First Amendment and free press issues.”

“Doesn’t that turn the law and regulation on its head?” the judge asked. “Subpoenas are the last step, not the first step.”

Subramanian added: “It’s a matter of just basic compliance to the law.”

Buckley contended there was an exception to those restrictions that allows the nation’s attorney general to approve intrusive subpoenas, but that only drew further rebuke from the judge after he read the statute.

“How is this an exception of the basic rule that’s literally two provisions above it?” Subramanian said.

He referred to the provision that says “the government should have made all reasonable attempts to obtain the information, communications records, or business records from alternative sources.”

The DOJ was placed yet again on the defensive when the judge demanded that prosecutors explain why they had also sought the communication records of two Times reporters’ spouses and another reporter’s mother.

“That was an error which we own,” Buckley said. “It was a consequence of us trying to move quickly.”

Subramanian then demanded to hear from Kevin Sullivan, a prosecutor who normally works on high-profile terrorism cases but was on this investigation’s team. The judge commanded Sullivan to get up from the gallery, where he was sitting with the crowd, and position himself at the prosecution team’s table.

Subramanian then questioned why Sullivan signed off on a subpoena on July 14 that stated the investigation was not public — days after the Times had already published a story about it.

“Your Honor, the wording was imprecise,” Sullivan said.

And when Sullivan tried to privately converse with his fellow prosecutors, the judge interrupted him with a “hold on!” Subramanian then asked Sullivan why his subpoena application to another judge made no mention that the supposedly non-public investigation was in fact a highly publicized and controversial national story involving the Times.

“Judge, it was an oversight on the government’s part,” Sullivan said, while throwing up both hands with a shrug.

Subramanian raised the possibility of personally holding the prosecutors accountable for misconduct, noting that, in a civil case, he would now be considering sanctions. He then turned back to Buckley.

“Are you still on this investigation?” he asked.

“Yes, Your Honor.”

“So, are you going to do this again?” the judge said.

“Absolutely not, Your Honor,” Buckley said.

Subramanian later pressed Buckley on how the senior prosecutor could make so many missteps while claiming to have already been familiar with the rules. Buckley then said he doesn’t “review every piece of paper” under his command.

Prosecutors called for a five-minute break, during which Buckley walked out of the courtroom. He was seen placing four phone calls and quickly typing messages on his phone as he paced along a window that faced Lower Manhattan.

When someone called him, Buckley ducked into a conference room. Once he was back in the courtroom, Buckley said the government was now prepared to “unilaterally withdraw” the subpoenas — but that the investigation would continue and that reporters might be subpoenaed again in the future.

“Moving forward, we’re not going to have the kinds of errors that have plagued this case so far?” the judge asked.

“No, your Honor,” Buckley said.

Subramanian then made Buckley “pledge” that he would follow the law and regulations, referring to the exchange as a necessary “soliloquy.”

David O’Neil, a Washington lawyer representing the newspaper, noted that “the record here is replete with bad faith.”

Buckley leaned into the microphone.

“We dispute any allegation of bad faith, and we’ll leave it at that.”

entries.title: Senate Democrats Ask Watchdog to Probe Trump Gutting Offshore Wind
entries.summary: Sen. Martin Heinrich asked the Government Accountability Office to review the Interior Department’s offshore wind leasing and permitting practices.
entries.content:
Senate Democrats are ramping up efforts to investigate the Trump administration’s push to shut down offshore wind development.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico), asked the Government Accountability Office to look into the Interior Department’s leasing and permitting practices for offshore wind.

“The Trump Administration has shown a strong willingness to go to any lengths to kill wind projects, including stretching the bounds of the law,” Heinrich, the top Democrat on the Senate’s Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, wrote to GAO. “It is imperative that Congress and the American people understand how DOI’s actions have crippled the development of wind energy in the country.”

The Government Accountability Office can decline requests from members of Congress, but requests from ranking members like Heinrich are prioritized.

Heinrich’s request comes after a group of senators launched an investigation into buyout agreements totaling almost $2.6 billion that halted offshore wind projects planned for waters off of Maine, New York and California.

The senators asked the companies that received those buyouts — TotalEnergies, Ocean Winds, Duke Energy and Invenergy — to respond to questions about their communications with the Trump administration by Aug, 6.

President Donald Trump has taken a sweeping approach to halting the offshore wind industry, temporarily withdrawing leases in U.S. waters, pausing projects, canceling funding, requiring heightened review by the Interior Department, and paying developers to cancel planned projects.

Federal judges have deemed several of those actions unlawful, including the halting of new leases and a requirement for the interior secretary to sign off on all wind and solar projects on federal lands and water.

The administration’s efforts to shut down clean-energy projects has become a sticking point in bipartisan discussions of permitting reform, which Heinrich is leading for Democrats along with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island).

Streamlining the permitting process for energy projects and other infrastructure is a priority for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, but longstanding partisan gridlock has made an agreement elusive.

entries.title: Trump Sidesteps SCOTUS With New Tariffs
entries.summary: The new tariffs range from 10% to 12.5%.
entries.content:
The Trump administration unveiled a new slate of global tariffs on Thursday, again circumventing the Supreme Court after it struck down President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariff policy earlier this year.

Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, said Thursday that the administration would use Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to place new tariffs on 60 countries. The tariffs would range from 10% to 12.5% and target multiple allies. Canada, Mexico, and the United Kingdom would be subject to a 10% tariff.

“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” Greer said in a statement.

The administration justified the tariffs by claiming that some of the countries have done too little to prevent the import of goods made with forced labor. Section 301 allows the administration to place tariffs in response to unfair, unjustifiable, or discriminatory foreign trade practices.

In February, the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to enact tariffs. The Trump administration then opted to use Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to levy a 10% global import tariff.

But those tariffs cannot be in place for more than 150 days and would expire on Friday without approval from Congress to extend them.

The new tariffs would have no expiration date and were announced just days after Trump said he would place a 50% tariff on some Canadian goods.

The renewed turbulence in the trade world comes just months before the midterm elections.

“[Section] 122 is really designed to be like an emergency power authority. I think they recognized they weren't going to keep this long term,” Andrew Siciliano, the global and U.S. head of trade and customs at KPMG, told NOTUS. “They were probably planning for six months to come up with a new mechanism to apply the tariffs.”

The administration’s abrupt shifts in tariff policy have complicated the broader global trade environment. Siciliano described it as “extremely disruptive,” but added that businesses are learning to anticipate and adjust.

entries.title: Three Airports Opt Into Trump Administration’s New Private Airport Security Model
entries.summary: The TSA workers’ union say the TSA Gold+ program “jeopardizes the safety of the flying public.”
entries.content:
Airports in Tampa, Des Moines and Charleston will be the first to opt into TSA Gold+, the Trump administration’s new initiative that allows private contractors to manage the screening and security processes.

Under the new program, the Transportation Security Administration is still in charge of oversight, but some industry leaders are calling the decision a “step backwards” for aviation security.

The American Federation of Government Employees, which represents TSA agents, denounced the expansion of these public-private partnerships.

“Make no mistake – this is a major departure and step backwards from the aviation screening security system that Congress created in the wake of the Sept. 11th terrorist attacks in 2001 and the deadly bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Scotland in 1988,” Everett Kelley, the national president of AFGE, said in a press release.

TSA announced the new program in May in an email sent to employees, and the agency recently began accepting applications from private contractors, due at the end of the month. The agency bypassed congressional approval by relying on existing statutory authorities found in the Screening Partnership Program launched by TSA in 2004.

The White House added $52 million to the fiscal year 2027 budget proposal to help advance the push for privatization in security and screening at airports — which includes a mandatory expansion of the SPP that could affect up to 220 of the nation’s 440 commercial airports, according to the AFGE.

“Changes of this magnitude should not be made behind closed doors without the input of Congress, the flying public, the local airport authorities, and TSA employees themselves,” Kelley said.

Tampa International Airport cited increased efficiency and the need to supplement their workforce during government shutdowns as reasons for opting into the program.

“The change to privatization not only reduces disruption risks caused by lapses in federal appropriations or government shutdowns but also allows greater flexibility in exploring new screening checkpoint infrastructure and technology to enhance the customer experience,” an airport spokesperson said.

Twenty airports across the country have used the SPP to fill gaps in their workforces during previous shutdowns, including earlier this year, when TSA agents worked without pay for 76 days during the partial government shutdown.

Des Moines International Airport praised the program’s potential to provide “leap forward in technology” at security checkpoints, but the airport also acknowledged the concerns current transportation security officers may have about adopting TSA Gold+.

"TSA officers have done an outstanding job serving Central Iowa, and we recognize there is uncertainty whenever a new program is discussed," Brian Mulcahy, CEO of the Des Moines Airport Authority, said in a press release.

“TSA Gold+ presents a new way for airports to deliver exceptional service to every traveler, while advancing security, efficiency, and the overall airport experience,” TSA said in a statement. “Throughout the transition of these airports, we remain committed to operational stability and supporting our employees.”

The Homeland Security Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Des Moines International Airport is set to adopt TSA Gold+ in January 2027, with Charleston International Airport following in February and Tampa International Airport in May, according to correspondence shared with NOTUS by the AFGE.

The labor union argued that the potential expansion into airports across the country not only impacts TSA employees but also the overall safety of the aviation system.

“The administration’s actions should concern all Americans, and AFGE will continue to speak out against any proposal that threatens our members’ jobs and jeopardizes the safety of the flying public,” Kelley said.

entries.title: Trump Expands His Ratepayer Pledge With Republican Governors, Utilities
entries.summary: The White House’s non-binding pledge encourages data centers to bring, build or buy their own power generation.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced Thursday an expansion of a pledge to protect ratepayers from increasing energy costs as power-hungry AI infrastructure springs up across the country.

Fifty-five utilities including Avangrid, Dominion, Entergy, NextEra and PG&E joined the pledge, along with 106 energy cooperatives, 28 data center developers and 23 governors — all Republicans. Seven AI companies had already signed on in March. Democratic governors Wes Moore of Maryland and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, who were involved in a previous White House agreement, were not part of the pledge.

Spokespeople for Shapiro and Moore said they were not invited to sign on to the pledge.

Companies that sign on to the pledge agree to build, bring or buy their own power supply, paying for the full cost of that energy and for the grid upgrades required to serve data centers. They also agree to pay for the power and grid upgrades whether they actually use the electricity or not.

The pledge, which is non-binding, also pushes companies to invest in local jobs and to contribute to grid resilience, making their backup generation systems available to prevent shortages and blackouts.

“It’s hard to believe, but you need double the electricity that we have right now, maybe even more than that, to really fulfill what you want to do,” Trump said at an EPA event announcing the expanded pledge. “We’re leading China by a lot, and using our old grid would not have worked.”

Republican Govs. Brian Kemp of Georgia, Jeff Landry of Louisiana, Brad Little of Idaho, and Jim Pillen of Nebraska spoke at the event, addressing recent pushback against local data center development across the country and highlighting the benefits to their residents.

Landry described an agreement between Richland Parish, Louisiana, and Meta that generated enough revenue to give teachers in that community five-figure bonuses.

“This is a moment where we get to protect our people, empower our communities and unleash unprecedented economic opportunity,” he said.

The Trump administration has aggressively pushed building data centers as part of its commitment to building the artificial intelligence industry in the United States. But several top officials have acknowledged the political backlash to rising utility rates stemming from their development.

This week at a summit for AI stakeholders both inside and outside the government, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the “noise” around data centers is “not going to slow the progress of artificial intelligence.” Americans overwhelmingly oppose data centers being built in their communities.

The implementation and enforcement of ratepayer protections is overwhelmingly the responsibility of states.

Jeff Dennis, executive director of the Electricity Customer Alliance, said the addition of utilities and governors to the pledge could push protections forward.

“I think it makes a meaningful difference in terms of the ability of the pledge to drive forward progress at the institutions that have the authority to actually give teeth to it,” he said.

Implementing and enforcing ratepayer protections would require state public utilities commissions, which regulate the rates utility companies charge customers, to step in.

Some states have already started to create large load tariffs — special contracts with big customers that can dictate which costs they pay, and whether they’ll pay for the cost of the power and upgrades to the grid built for their needs, even if they don’t use it all.

But the major tenet of the pledge — the push for data centers to bring their own power to the table — has been harder to work out, Dennis said.

“It's notable that utilities have joined the ratepayer pledge in this regard because utilities take a few different positions on whether their customers can actually participate in the market directly in that way to procure their own power,” he said. “We'll be interested to see how utilities that have signed this pledge go about implementing that specific piece.”

entries.title: House Republicans Focus on Democrats' Plans, Not Their Own Wins
entries.summary: Republicans admit messaging on their own tax bill has been challenging, so they are warning voters about what Democrats would mean to their pocketbooks.
entries.content:
House Republican leaders are kicking off their summer campaign blitz warning voters about how Democrats’ policies will increase their taxes instead of touting their own signature tax cut bill.

The strategy highlights the difficulties GOP lawmakers face when it comes to voters feeling the economic benefits of their policies.

“What’s really important as relates to the tax code is to contrast what we’ve done to help make life more affordable for families and put more money in their pocket versus what the Democrats would do,” Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) told reporters on Thursday ahead of a weekslong summer recess.

Republicans passed a party-line package to extend and make permanent President Donald Trump’s 2017 tax cuts. Since then, they have struggled to make the marquee legislation an effective pitch to voters as they look to retain their slim majority.

“Do we communicate our ideas great all the time? That's been a fault of the Republican Party,” Scalise acknowledged.

Instead, Republicans are highlighting the far-left insurgence within the Democratic Party, often referring to Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates as “communists.” And in many cases working to paint the entire party as extreme leftist.

This approach differs from what some members competing in purple districts say they’d prefer to emphasize, even as top leaders fan out to those contests this summer.

“We’ll focus exclusively on the issues that matter to people, from affordability and the cost of living, and what we’ve done on taxes and housing. Obviously, energy costs, and not just gas, but utilities,” Rep. Mike Lawler, (R-New York), who represents a district Kamala Harris won in 2024, told NOTUS.

Lawler faces Cait Conley, a military veteran who Democrats note is running slightly ahead of Lawler in polling.

Republicans have seized on recent primaries in New York City where voters voted for Mayor Zohran Mamdani and a handful of democratic socialist who beat out Democrats who were viewed as establishment candidates.

Speaker Mike Johnson and Scalise have plans to visit New York state in August.

Rep. Derrick Van Orden, whose Wisconsin district became more competitive this cycle, according to Cook Political Report’s rating, said he’ll be traveling the district on his Harley talking about “gas, groceries and grandkids” and hopes leadership does the same.

Another Republican in a tight race, Pennsylvania Rep. John Bresnahan, said leaders should focus on affordability but also speak to issues important to northeast Pennsylvania such as eradicating an Obama-era storm water management fee levied on homeowners.

“Absolutely, we could talk about no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security,” Bresnahan said. “These are all incredible things that we could take back home.”

When asked if Democrats’ proposals should be part of their talking points, he indicated yes.

“He could certainly talk about some of the communism ideology that seems to be infiltrating the Democrat Party right now,” Bresnahan said about Scalise.

Democrats, meanwhile, accused Republicans of making them the scapegoat for rising living costs. They’re planning their own campaign pitch to voters starting this Sunday.

“The do nothing Republican Congress has been a complete and total disaster. Costs haven’t gone down. Costs have gone up. Gas prices are out of control. The war in Iran is spiraling, and they continue to try to divert blame onto us,” Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told NOTUS. “The American people aren’t buying it.”
